items.meta: Own mineral rights in Antrim County, home ground of the Antrim Shale. Straight talk on what a mature-decline interest is actually worth today. Get an offer.

sections.html:
The Antrim Shale is named after this county because the rock was first worked here, and if your family still owns minerals under a farm or a cottage lot in Antrim County, you're sitting on the original play, not the hype around it.

Antrim County, Michigan, county seat Bellaire, gave its name to the Antrim Shale, the Devonian-age gas shale that got drilled hard across the northern Lower Peninsula from the late 1980s through the 1990s. That matters because it means the wells here are old. Not old like risky. Old like mature, dewatered, and past the steep part of the decline curve. If you inherited a mineral interest or a small royalty check tied to land in this county, you're not looking at a boom-time story. You're looking at a stripper-well story, and that's a different conversation than what most of the mailbox-offer letters pretend it is.

We buy and evaluate mineral and royalty interests across Antrim County, from the Elk Lake and Torch Lake corridor down through Central Lake and Ellsworth to the farm ground around Mancelona. Some of that land is resort property now. Some of it's still working farm and forest. Either way, the mineral estate under it was frequently severed decades before the current surface owner ever bought the place, which is exactly why so many owners in this county have never met the operator producing their gas.

sections.title: Why this county is the actual Antrim play
sections.html:
The Antrim Shale isn't a marketing name, it's a real stratigraphic unit that outcrops and was first tested in this part of Michigan, and Antrim County sits inside the historic core of the trend along with Otsego, Kalkaska, and Montmorency counties. The gas is biogenic, meaning bacteria produced it in the rock rather than heat and pressure cooking organic material the way conventional gas forms. It sits shallow, often between 600 and 2,200 feet, and it flows out of natural fractures once the wells have been dewatered long enough to drop the water table around the wellbore.

Operators here historically included names like Ward Lake Energy, Miller Exploration, and Belden and Blake before a lot of that Antrim acreage rolled up into larger holding companies over the years. If your royalty statement shows a company name you don't recognize, that's normal. These interests have changed hands through mergers more than once since the original lease was signed.

sections.title: What ownership actually looks like around here
sections.html:
A lot of Antrim County mineral ownership traces back to farm patents and family land that got carved up over generations, plus a fair amount of resort and cottage development around Torch Lake and Elk Lake where the surface sold off separate from the minerals decades ago. That's a split estate, and it's common up here. You can own a fractional mineral interest under a lakefront lot you've never even seen the deed reference for, because the severance happened before your branch of the family bought or inherited the surface.

The other common situation is heirship. A grandparent or great-uncle held a mineral interest, it never got formally divided at death, and now three or four cousins are each getting a small check, or nobody's getting anything because the interest sits unclaimed at the register of deeds. Antrim County's register of deeds office in Bellaire is where you'd start pulling the chain of title if you're not sure what you actually own.

sections.title: Why the checks are smaller than what your parents remember
sections.html:
This is the part we're not going to dance around. Antrim Shale wells in this county are decades into production now, most drilled during the tax-credit boom of the late 1980s and 1990s. Biogenic shale gas wells have a notoriously long, flat decline once they get past the early dewatering phase, but flat and long doesn't mean strong. A well that made real money in 1994 can be producing a fraction of that now, and a royalty check that used to run real money a month can be down to something you'd barely notice hitting the bank.

That's not a sign something's wrong with your interest. It's just where a mature Antrim well sits on the curve at this point. Anybody offering you a number based on what these wells did twenty-five years ago is either not doing the homework or hoping you won't check.

We pull recent production history against your interest, look at current operator activity in your section, township, and range, and weigh that against your actual royalty statements, not what a well did at its peak. Value on a mature, low-decline interest depends heavily on how many net mineral acres you hold, whether the well is still economic to operate, and whether there's any chance of a future workover or offset drilling nearby. We'll tell you plainly if your interest is worth holding for the small steady check versus taking a lump sum now.

There's no guaranteed number we can quote before we've seen your statements and run the numbers, and anyone who quotes you a per-acre price sight unseen is guessing or angling for a signature.

That's the nature of a mature well, not a red flag on your interest specifically.

sections.title: What's Actually Under Rapid City
sections.html:
This end of Kalkaska County sits inside the Antrim Shale core — the Devonian black shale that made northern Michigan a gas play in the 1980s and '90s. It's shallow, usually somewhere between 500 and 2,000 feet, and it's biogenic gas, meaning bacteria did the work over geologic time rather than heat and pressure cooking oil into gas the way it happens in West Texas. That matters for one big reason: Antrim wells come on producing a decent stream of gas and water, then decline hard and fast in the first few years before settling into a long, low, flat tail that can run for decades.

If your well was drilled in the late '80s or '90s boom, it's probably sitting on that flat tail right now. Small checks, but steady ones — and that steadiness is worth something to a buyer even when the monthly number looks unimpressive on paper.

sections.title: Why Your Royalty Check Doesn't Match What Grandpa Got

We hear this complaint constantly around Kalkaska County: the well used to pay a lot more. It did. Antrim decline curves are steep up front and that's not the operator shorting you — it's the physics of a shallow biogenic reservoir depleting. What's left now is late-life production, and late-life production gets valued differently than a fresh well. A buyer looking at your interest isn't pricing it off what the well made in 1994. They're pricing it off what's realistic for the next 10 to 20 years, discounted back to today.

You inherited a mineral interest, a stack of old paperwork, and zero explanation, and now you're the one who has to figure out what any of it means.

It happens the same way in almost every Michigan family. Somebody passes, the estate gets settled, and buried in the paperwork is a mineral interest nobody talked about at Thanksgiving, tied to land up in Antrim or Otsego or Kalkaska County that the family hasn't had a physical connection to in decades. Maybe there's a check history. Maybe the checks stopped years ago and nobody knows why. You've got three real options once you're holding an inherited interest: keep it and start managing it yourself, sell it and take the cash, or ignore it and let the paperwork keep piling up until the next generation inherits the same confusion. None of those is automatically the right call. It depends on what the interest is actually producing, how many other heirs you're splitting it with, and whether you want to be the person fielding division order updates and 1099s for a fraction of a well you've never seen.

sections.title: First, Figure Out What You Actually Inherited

This tells you the legal description, your exact fractional share if there are multiple heirs, and whether the interest was ever formally transferred into your name with the operator. A surprising number of inherited interests are still sitting in a deceased relative's name with the operator years after probate closed, which means checks aren't being issued to anyone, or worse, are getting flagged and routed to state unclaimed property.

sections.title: Multiple Heirs Complicates Everything
sections.html: If you're one of four siblings who each inherited a quarter of the same interest, you've now got four separate, smaller fractional shares where there used to be one. Each heir has to be updated individually with the operator, each gets their own 1099, and if one sibling wants to sell and three want to keep it, that's an awkward conversation nobody scheduled. Some families sell the whole interest together and split proceeds cleanly through the estate, which sidesteps the ongoing coordination problem entirely. Others let each heir decide individually, since a mineral interest can typically be sold in fractional pieces without every co-owner agreeing. Neither path is wrong, but it's worth deciding as a family rather than defaulting into confusion.

sections.title: Weighing Keep vs. Sell
sections.html:
If the well is a strong, actively managed Antrim or Niagaran unit still throwing off decent checks, and you don't mind the small ongoing paperwork, keeping it can make sense, especially if you view it as a long-term family asset rather than a hassle. If the well is deep into decline, the checks are trivial, or you'd genuinely rather have a lump sum than a decades-long trickle from an asset tied to land you've never set foot on, selling converts an inherited obligation into a clean, one-time number. There's no moral high ground either direction. It's a financial and lifestyle decision, and the honest starting point is knowing what the interest is actually worth right now, not guessing based on what it made in some good year decades back.

One more thing worth saying plainly: if you inherited an interest and someone shows up fast with an unsolicited offer before you've even confirmed the title, slow down. That doesn't mean the offer is bad, but a fair buyer will wait while you confirm what you actually own.

faqs.q: Do you need to formally transfer the mineral interest into your name?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want to receive royalty checks and eventually sell cleanly. The operator needs a recorded deed or probate document showing you as the current owner, or checks may stop, get held, or route to state unclaimed property under the previous owner's name.

faqs.q: How do you know if the inherited interest is worth anything?
faqs.a: Pull recent royalty history if there is any, confirm the well's operator and current production status, and get a straight valuation before assuming anything. Some inherited Michigan interests are dry paperwork, others are quietly still producing and were simply never actively managed by the previous owner.

faqs.q: Can you sell your share if your siblings want to keep theirs?
faqs.a: Generally yes. A fractional mineral interest can typically be sold independently of what co-owning heirs decide to do with their own shares, though it's worth confirming there's no restriction in the specific deed or estate documents first.

faqs.q: What if the mineral interest was never mentioned in probate?
faqs.a: That happens more than people expect, especially with small legacy interests that got overlooked. If you suspect there's an unaddressed mineral interest tied to a deceased relative's Michigan land, a title search at the county register of deeds is the place to start confirming it.

items.name: Got an Unsolicited Offer?
items.meta: Received an unsolicited letter offering to buy your Michigan mineral rights? Get a second, straight opinion before signing anything back.

sections.html:
A letter shows up out of nowhere offering to buy your mineral rights, with a number, a deadline, and a return envelope already stamped, and something about it feels off.

Mailbox offers are a real business model in Michigan mineral country, and they're not automatically a scam, but they're built to work in the buyer's favor, not yours. Somebody pulls county records, identifies mineral owners tied to a producing or leased tract, and blankets them with letters offering a flat number, sometimes with language designed to feel urgent, sign by this date, offer subject to change, act now. The company sending it usually knows more about your interest's actual production than you do, because they've done the same research on hundreds of owners before mailing that letter.

That imbalance is the whole game. They know the well's production. You probably don't, or don't know how to read it if you have the statements sitting in a drawer. The honest move before signing anything back is getting an independent read on what the interest is actually worth, from someone who isn't the party trying to buy it from you at a number they picked.

sections.title: Why the First Number Is Rarely the Best Number
sections.html: Mailbox offer companies typically build in significant margin because they're buying blind, at scale, off a form letter, without you ever asking a follow-up question. That's the business model, cast a wide net, offer a number well below what careful analysis would support, and bank on some percentage of recipients just signing because the process feels easy and the deadline feels real. Some owners who sign are fine with that trade-off, easy over optimal. But you should at least know the gap exists before deciding it's a trade-off you're willing to make.

sections.title: What to Actually Check Before Responding
sections.html: Pull your own recent royalty statements and look at the multi-year trend instead of only the last check. Confirm who's currently operating the well and whether there's been any recent activity, permits, workovers, new units nearby, that might affect value. Check the legal description on the offer letter against your actual documented interest, because mailbox offers sometimes misstate the fraction or the tract, banking on owners not catching the discrepancy. And get a second opinion on value from a buyer who isn't the one who sent you the letter, so you're comparing their number against something independent rather than deciding in a vacuum.

sections.title: There's No Real Deadline
sections.html:
Legitimate mineral value doesn't expire on a Tuesday because a letter says so. If an offer includes pressure language, respond by this date or the offer is withdrawn, that's a sales tactic, not a reflection of the market moving. A real buyer will still want your interest next week or next month if the well's production hasn't changed. Taking a few days to check the offer against an independent valuation costs you nothing and protects you from signing away an interest for less than it's worth because a deadline felt real.

We'll look at any offer letter you've received and tell you straight whether it's in a reasonable range or well under what the interest supports, based on the well's actual production, not what the letter claims. If our number comes in close to theirs, we'll say so. If it's meaningfully different, you'll know before you sign anything back.

faqs.q: Are mailbox offers on mineral rights usually scams?
faqs.a: Not usually outright scams, but they're typically built with significant margin in the buyer's favor, sent at scale to owners who may not know how to independently value their own interest. The offer itself may be legitimate, just lower than a well-informed owner would accept.

faqs.q: Should you respond before the deadline on the offer letter?
faqs.a: No. Deadlines on unsolicited mineral offers are almost always a sales tactic, not a reflection of real market timing. Take time to check the offer against an independent valuation before responding to anything.

faqs.q: How do you know if an unsolicited offer is a fair price?
faqs.a: Get a second opinion based on your recent royalty statements and the well's actual production trend from a source other than the company that sent the offer. Comparing two independent numbers tells you far more than evaluating one offer in isolation.

faqs.q: What if the offer letter has your mineral fraction wrong?
faqs.a: That happens, since these letters are often generated from incomplete or outdated county records. Confirm the legal description and your fractional interest against the actual county record before responding to any offer that references your interest.

faqs.q: Is it rude or risky to just not respond to a mailbox offer?
faqs.a: Not at all. There's no obligation to respond to an unsolicited letter, and ignoring it costs you nothing. If a buyer's terms sound reasonable once you've checked their number independently, you can always reach back out on your own timeline.

faqs.q: Do you need a lawyer before signing a mineral rights purchase agreement?
faqs.a: Not always for a straightforward sale, but it's a reasonable step if the acreage is complex, the offer is large, or the paperwork uses language you don't fully understand. A quick attorney review costs little compared to signing away an interest you didn't fully grasp.

items.name: Fractional & Small Interests
items.meta: Own a 1/16th, 1/32nd, or smaller mineral interest in Michigan? Find out if that fractional Antrim share is actually worth selling before you write it off.

sections.html:
A 1/64th interest in a well up in Otsego County sounds like nothing until you actually check what it's throwing off, and by then most owners have already decided it's not worth the paperwork.

Michigan's Antrim boom in the eighties and nineties spread ownership across families the same way most old plays do: land gets passed down, minerals get split among heirs, and three generations later a great-grandkid in another state owns a fraction of a fraction of an original tract. It's not unusual to see interests down at 1/32nd, 1/64th, even smaller, tied to a well that's been producing since before the current owner was born. A lot of these owners have never sold because the checks are small enough that nobody's bothered to look closer, or because they assume a fractional interest that tiny can't possibly be worth the effort to sell.

Sometimes that assumption is right. A dust-dry fractional share of a nearly depleted well genuinely might not be worth much. But sometimes it's wrong, and the only way to know is to actually look at recent production, confirm the exact fraction you hold against the county record, and get a real number instead of guessing based on how small the check looks on paper.

sections.title: Why Small Doesn't Mean Worthless
sections.html: The size of your fraction and the value of your interest aren't the same thing. A 1/64th interest in a strong producing unit can be worth more than a 1/4 interest in a well that's basically stripper production at this point. What actually drives value is the well's current production, how many net mineral acres your fraction represents, remaining reserves, and who's operating the unit. Owners get hung up on the fraction itself as if it's the whole story, when it's really just one input into a bigger calculation.

sections.title: The Paperwork Problem Fractional Owners Face
sections.html: Small interests carry outsized paperwork burden relative to what they pay out. You still get a 1099 every year no matter how small the check is. You still need to keep the operator updated if you move, or the checks stop and end up in state unclaimed property instead of your mailbox. If there are multiple heirs holding pieces of the same original interest, someone has to coordinate updates, changes of address, and eventually another round of division when an heir passes and their share splits again. For a lot of owners, the administrative weight of a tiny interest outweighs what it actually pays, and that's a legitimate reason to consider selling separate from whatever the raw dollar value comes out to.

sections.title: Confirming What You Actually Own
sections.html:
Before pricing anything, we confirm the legal description and your exact fractional share against the county register of deeds record in whichever Michigan county the minerals sit in. Old family paperwork sometimes lists a fraction that doesn't match the current recorded interest, especially after multiple generations of heirship and probate. It's common to find that what a family believed was a 1/16th interest is actually smaller after later generations split it further, or occasionally larger if a sibling's share reverted. Getting that number right matters because it's the multiplier on everything else in the valuation.

This is also where we catch interests that are producing but the owner never realized it, because the checks were going to an old address or a deceased relative's name and got redirected to state unclaimed property instead of the current heir. If you inherited a fractional interest and have never seen a check, that's worth checking before assuming the interest is dry.

faqs.q: Is a 1/64th mineral interest even worth selling?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on what that fraction represents in current production and net mineral acres, not the fraction itself. Some small interests in active units are worth real money. Others in depleted wells aren't. The only way to know is to check recent production against your confirmed share.

faqs.q: How do you find out your exact fractional share?
faqs.a: Start with the county register of deeds in the Michigan county where the minerals are located, cross-referenced against any division order the operator sent you. Family paperwork passed down through heirs isn't always accurate after multiple generations of splitting.

faqs.q: Why haven't you ever received a royalty check on your interest?
faqs.a: A few common reasons: the well isn't currently producing, your address was never updated with the operator after you inherited, or your share was too small to trigger a check under the operator's minimum payment threshold and is accruing or sitting with the state as unclaimed property.

faqs.q: Does it cost anything to find out what your fractional interest is worth?
faqs.a: No. We review your documentation and recent production history and give you a straight answer, and there's no obligation to sell if the number or the situation doesn't work for you.

faqs.q: Can you sell your fractional interest without the other heirs agreeing?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes. A fractional undivided interest is generally your own to sell regardless of what co-owning heirs decide to do with their shares, though it's worth checking your specific deed or estate paperwork for any unusual restrictions before assuming that's the case for you.

items.name: Minerals in Probate & Estates
items.meta: Handling a Michigan estate with mineral rights and need to sell as executor? Here's how probate mineral sales actually work, and why timing matters for closing.

sections.html:
You're the executor, the estate has a Michigan mineral interest nobody in the family knows what to do with, and probate court wants the estate settled, not sitting open.

Executors get handed a lot of unfamiliar assets during estate settlement, and a fractional mineral interest tied to some Michigan county the deceased never talked about is one of the more confusing ones. Unlike a house or a bank account, there's no obvious market to check, no realtor to call, and the value isn't printed on a statement the way it is for a brokerage account. But probate court still expects the estate's assets accounted for and distributed, and a mineral interest is real property that has to be handled the same as everything else in the estate.

The good news is that selling a mineral interest during probate isn't complicated once you know the steps. It typically requires confirming the executor's authority through the letters testamentary or letters of administration, getting a valuation on the interest, and either distributing it to heirs or selling it and distributing proceeds, depending on what the will or the heirs decide. We handle probate sales regularly and can work directly with the estate attorney on documentation, which is usually the fastest way through it.

sections.title: Confirming Executor Authority to Sell
sections.html: Before any sale, the buyer needs to see the letters testamentary or letters of administration issued by the probate court naming you as executor or personal representative with authority over the estate's assets. If the will specifically addresses mineral or oil and gas interests, that language matters too. Some estates require court approval for a sale of real property depending on how the will is structured or whether it's an intestate estate, so it's worth confirming with the estate attorney what's actually required in your specific probate matter before assuming a straightforward sale is possible.

sections.title: Sell Now or Distribute to Heirs First
sections.html: Executors generally have two paths. Sell the mineral interest as part of settling the estate and distribute cash proceeds to the heirs per the will or intestate succession, which is usually the cleaner option when heirs are scattered, disagree on what to do with the interest, or simply want the estate closed without carrying forward a shared asset. Or, distribute the interest itself to heirs as tenants in common and let them decide individually whether to keep or sell their share, which can drag the resolution out but keeps decision-making with the family rather than the executor. Which path makes sense usually comes down to whether the heirs are aligned or not, and how quickly the estate needs to close.

sections.title: Working with the Estate Attorney
sections.html:
We're happy to work directly with the estate's attorney rather than routing everything through the executor personally, which keeps the sale properly documented for the court record and reduces the burden on whoever's already juggling the rest of the estate's business. A written valuation and purchase agreement referencing the probate case number and the executor's authority is standard, and most probate courts are familiar with mineral interest sales as part of estate settlement even if they don't see them every day.

One thing worth flagging early: if the deceased owned the interest for decades, the estate may need to establish a stepped-up basis for tax purposes based on date-of-death value, which matters for the heirs' eventual tax treatment whether they keep or sell. That's a conversation for the estate's CPA or attorney, not something we advise on, but it's worth raising with them before the sale closes rather than after.

faqs.q: Can an executor sell mineral rights without heir approval?
faqs.a: It depends on the will's language and Michigan probate requirements for the specific estate. Some executors have broad authority to sell estate assets; others need court approval or heir consent depending on how the estate is structured. Check with the estate attorney before proceeding.

faqs.q: What documents do you need as executor to sell a mineral interest?
faqs.a: Typically the letters testamentary or letters of administration from probate court, and any will language addressing the mineral or oil and gas interest specifically. We can work directly with your estate attorney to confirm exactly what's needed for your case.

faqs.q: Should you sell the mineral rights or distribute them to heirs?
faqs.a: That depends on whether the heirs agree on what to do. Selling and distributing cash proceeds is usually simpler when heirs are scattered or disagree. Distributing the interest itself keeps the decision with the family but can drag out estate closing.

faqs.q: Does selling during probate affect the heirs' taxes?
faqs.a: Inherited assets typically get a stepped-up basis to date-of-death value, which affects capital gains treatment. Talk to the estate's CPA or tax advisor about how that applies to your specific situation before the sale closes.

faqs.q: How long does a probate mineral sale usually take to close?
faqs.a: It varies by how quickly the estate attorney can confirm executor authority and by whether the specific probate court requires additional approval for the sale. Once documentation is in hand, the transaction itself typically moves faster than most other estate real property sales.

items.name: Leased but Undrilled
items.meta: Signed a Michigan mineral lease years ago and no well's ever been drilled? Here's what your undrilled leased interest is actually worth and why timing matters.

sections.html:
You cashed a bonus check years ago, signed a lease, and then nothing happened. No rig, no royalty, just an old document sitting in a drawer.

Getting leased and staying undrilled is a common story across Michigan mineral country, especially outside the tightest core of the Antrim and Niagaran plays. An operator or a landman working for one leased your acreage during an active period, paid a signing bonus, locked in the terms, and then the drilling never came, or came somewhere else in the unit and left your specific tract untouched. Now you're holding a lease that may or may not still be in its primary term, may or may not have quietly expired, and you have no royalty income to show for it beyond that original bonus check.

The value question here is different from a producing well, because there's no royalty history to run the numbers on. What you've actually got is a bet on future drilling, and that bet is worth something real, just priced differently than a producing interest. Whether it's worth much depends heavily on whether the lease is still active, what's happening on nearby tracts, and whether the operator holding your lease has shown any recent interest in the acreage at all.

sections.title: Check Whether the Lease Is Even Still Alive
sections.html: Michigan oil and gas leases typically run a primary term, three or five years is common, and unless the operator has drilled a well on the leased tract or the unit it's pooled into, paid delay rentals on schedule, or extended the term some other way spelled out in the lease, the lease can lapse on its own. A lot of owners assume a lease from fifteen years ago is still binding when it actually expired years back, which means the minerals reverted to unencumbered ownership without anyone telling the owner. That's worth checking at the county register of deeds before assuming you're still tied to whoever originally leased the tract, because an expired lease changes your options considerably.

sections.title: What Drives Value on Undrilled Acreage
sections.html: Without production history, value comes down to geology and activity. Where does your tract sit relative to the productive core of the Antrim or Niagaran reef trend? Have nearby units seen recent drilling, permits, or renewed leasing activity? Is the operator holding your lease still an active player in Michigan, or a smaller outfit that hasn't drilled anything in the state in years? An undrilled tract sitting inside an active area with recent nearby permits is worth meaningfully more than the same acreage sitting on the fringe with an operator that's gone quiet. This is exactly the kind of judgment call that requires actually looking at the surrounding activity, not applying a flat number to every undrilled tract.

sections.title: Selling Undrilled Minerals vs. Waiting It Out
sections.html:
Some owners hold undrilled minerals for decades hoping a well eventually gets drilled and the royalty starts flowing. In a mature basin like Michigan's, where a lot of the easy, obvious drilling already happened decades ago, that wait can be long, and there's no promise it ever pays off. Others would rather take a number now for the acreage's speculative value and stop waiting on something that may never come. If your lease is close to expiring with no drilling activity in sight, that's also worth factoring in, because once it lapses your minerals become unencumbered, which can actually be a better selling position since a buyer isn't inheriting someone else's lease terms.

There's no dishonest way to price undrilled minerals as a sure thing, and anyone quoting you a confident number without checking recent activity in your area is skipping a step. A fair valuation on leased-but-undrilled acreage says plainly that it's speculative and prices it against comparable activity, not against a well that doesn't exist.

faqs.q: Is your mineral lease still active if no well was ever drilled?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Most Michigan oil and gas leases have a primary term and lapse if no well is drilled and no delay rentals were paid to extend it. Check the lease's original term dates against the county register of deeds record to confirm whether it's still binding.

faqs.q: What's an undrilled mineral interest actually worth?
faqs.a: There's no production history to price against, so value depends on the tract's position relative to active drilling nearby, recent permit activity in the area, and whether the leasing operator is still active in Michigan. It's speculative value, priced against comparable recent activity, not a guaranteed number.

faqs.q: Should you wait for a well to be drilled before selling?
faqs.a: That's a real option, but in a mature basin like Michigan's there's no promise drilling ever happens on your specific tract. If you'd rather have a current number than an open-ended wait, that's a legitimate reason to sell now instead of holding on speculation.

faqs.q: What happens if your lease expires with no drilling?
faqs.a: The minerals typically revert to unencumbered ownership, meaning no operator holds rights to drill until a new lease is signed. That can actually strengthen your position when selling, since a buyer isn't stepping into someone else's existing lease terms.

items.name: Non-Producing Minerals
items.meta: Own Michigan mineral rights with no well nearby and no lease in place? Non-producing doesn't mean worthless. Get a straight read before assuming it's nothing.

sections.html:
No well, no lease, no check ever, and now you're wondering if the mineral rights sitting under your family's old Michigan land are worth anything at all.

A lot of mineral owners in Michigan hold acreage that's never seen a drill bit and isn't currently under lease to anyone. Maybe it's outside the core Antrim or Niagaran reef trend and just never got the attention that busier counties saw. Maybe it was leased once decades ago and that lease lapsed with nothing to show for it. Maybe it's simply been sitting quiet since the original severance and nobody's ever come knocking. Whatever the history, non-producing minerals sit in a strange spot: there's no royalty check to point to as proof of value, and no history to run numbers against.

That doesn't mean the interest is worthless, and it doesn't mean it's a hidden goldmine either. It means the value question has to be answered differently, based on geology, nearby activity, and whether there's any reasonable chance of future leasing interest, rather than actual production. Some non-producing tracts genuinely aren't worth much right now. Others sit close enough to active development that a buyer will still pay real money for the speculative position. The only way to know which one you're holding is to actually look.

sections.title: Why Non-Producing Isn't the Same as Worthless
sections.html: Buyers who acquire mineral positions across a region aren't only buying producing royalty streams. Some are building a book of acreage in areas they expect to see leasing activity return to, betting that consolidation, technology, or commodity price shifts eventually bring drilling back to areas that have been quiet for years. If your non-producing tract sits reasonably close to the Antrim core or along the Niagaran reef trend, there may be real interest even without a current well. If it's well outside any historically productive area, the honest answer is that speculative interest will be limited and the number will reflect that.

sections.title: What We Actually Check
sections.html: We look at where your tract sits relative to historically productive units, whether there's been any recent permitting or leasing activity on adjacent or nearby land, whether your minerals have ever been leased before and what those terms looked like, and the county record to confirm your ownership and legal description are clean. This isn't guesswork dressed up as analysis. It's the same due diligence any serious buyer runs before quoting a number, and it's the only honest way to value acreage without a production history to lean on.

sections.title: Holding vs. Selling Non-Producing Minerals
sections.html:
Some owners hold non-producing minerals indefinitely because there's no urgency and no cost to just leaving it alone, which is a reasonable position if you're not counting on the interest for anything and don't mind the small chance a lease offer shows up someday. Others would rather take a real number now, especially if the acreage sits in an area with limited near-term drilling prospects and the wait could stretch for years or never resolve. There's also a practical side: non-producing minerals still show up in estate paperwork for whoever inherits them next, and some owners would rather simplify that inheritance now than pass along an asset with an uncertain future to their kids.

If you decide to sell, expect the number to be modest relative to a producing interest, because you're selling speculative upside, not cash flow. That's not a lowball tactic, that's just what unproven acreage is worth. Anyone offering you producing-well money for non-producing minerals with no lease and no nearby activity is either mistaken about your tract or not being straight with you.

faqs.q: Can you sell mineral rights that have never produced anything?
faqs.a: Yes. Non-producing minerals are bought and sold regularly, priced against location relative to active plays and any recent leasing or permit activity nearby rather than production history. The number will be smaller than for a producing interest, but the acreage still has real value if it's positioned reasonably.

faqs.q: Is your non-producing interest worth more if it's near an active well?
faqs.a: Generally yes. Proximity to recent drilling, permitting, or active leasing suggests operators still see potential in the area, which supports better speculative value than acreage sitting well outside any recent activity.

faqs.q: Should you try to get your minerals leased before selling?
faqs.a: You can, but there's no guarantee an operator will lease acreage outside current areas of interest, and waiting on a lease that may never come can tie up the decision for years. Selling the non-producing interest as-is is often the more practical path if you'd rather not wait indefinitely.

faqs.q: How do you know if your land is near the Antrim or Niagaran trend?
faqs.a: We check your legal description against the historically productive areas of the play and any recent nearby permit activity when we review your interest. That comparison is the real basis for a fair number, not a guess based on the county name alone.

faqs.q: What if your minerals were leased once but the lease expired?
faqs.a: An expired lease with no drilling means your minerals reverted to unencumbered, non-producing status. That prior lease history is still useful information for a valuation, since it shows an operator once had enough interest to lease the tract, even if drilling never followed.

items.name: Out-of-State Owners
items.meta: Live outside Michigan but own mineral rights in Antrim, Otsego, or another county? Sell without a site visit, courthouse trip, or dealing with an out-of-state operator.

sections.html:
You live in Florida or Arizona or wherever the family scattered to, and somewhere back in Michigan there's a mineral interest nobody's physically checked on in years.

Out-of-state ownership is the rule, not the exception, in Michigan mineral country. Families who once worked land in Antrim or Otsego or Kalkaska County moved for jobs, retired somewhere warmer, or just spread out over a couple generations, and the mineral interest stayed put on the land while the owners didn't. Now you're managing a Michigan asset from a mailbox in another state, dealing with an operator you've never met in person, and every piece of paperwork, tax season, address changes, occasional operator correspondence, has to happen long-distance.

That distance creates real friction that in-state owners don't deal with. You can't easily drive to the county register of deeds to pull a record. You're not fielding calls from local landmen who might have useful information about nearby activity. And if you decide you want to sell, you're relying entirely on whatever documentation you can access remotely to prove what you own. None of that is a dealbreaker, but it does mean the process needs to work without requiring you to show up in Michigan in person, and not every buyer is set up to handle that smoothly.

sections.title: What Distance Actually Complicates
sections.html: The biggest practical issue for out-of-state owners is staying current with the operator. Address changes get missed, mail gets delayed or lost in a move, and checks below a certain threshold get held or diverted to state unclaimed property when correspondence bounces. If you've moved even once since you started owning the interest and never confirmed the operator has your current address, it's worth checking directly, because Michigan has its own unclaimed property database separate from wherever you currently live, and money sitting there doesn't come find you automatically.

sections.title: Selling Without Setting Foot in Michigan
sections.html: You don't need to travel to Michigan to sell a mineral interest, and any process that requires it is unnecessarily slow. Title work happens through the county register of deeds records directly, documentation can move by mail or electronically, and closing on a sale is handled through standard remote paperwork the same way real estate closings routinely happen across state lines. We work with out-of-state owners on this basis regularly, because most Antrim and Niagaran interests are held by people who don't live anywhere near the county the minerals sit in anymore.

sections.title: Why Absentee Ownership Sometimes Tips the Scale Toward Selling
sections.html:
There's a practical case for selling that's specific to out-of-state owners even beyond the raw valuation number. Managing a small, declining royalty interest from a thousand miles away, chasing paperwork, updating addresses, tracking 1099s for tax season in a state you don't live in, carries a real time cost that in-state owners don't feel as acutely. Some owners are perfectly happy to keep collecting a modest check regardless of distance. Others find that the hassle of remote administration outweighs what the interest actually pays, especially on a small fractional share, and would rather take a clean number and stop tracking a Michigan mailbox from the other side of the country.

Neither choice is wrong. But if distance is part of what's pushing you toward selling, that's a legitimate factor, not something to feel odd about weighing alongside the dollar figure.

faqs.q: Do you have to travel to Michigan to sell your mineral rights?
faqs.a: No. Title work is done through county records directly, and closing paperwork can be handled remotely by mail or electronically, the same way out-of-state real estate transactions are routinely closed without either party traveling.

faqs.q: How do you check if the operator has your correct address?
faqs.a: Your most recent royalty statement or division order should show the address on file. If checks have stopped or you've moved without updating the operator, contact them directly, and also check Michigan's state unclaimed property database in case checks were redirected there.

faqs.q: Is it harder to confirm ownership when you live out of state?
faqs.a: Not really, since county register of deeds records in Michigan are accessible without an in-person visit, though it can take longer than it would for a local owner. That's part of what we handle when reviewing your interest, so you don't have to track it down yourself.

faqs.q: Should you sell just because managing it remotely is a hassle?
faqs.a: That's a legitimate factor to weigh alongside the actual value, not a separate justification you need to defend. Some out-of-state owners are fine with the occasional paperwork. Others would rather have a clean number and stop tracking a Michigan interest from a distance.

faqs.q: Will you owe Michigan state taxes on the sale if you don't live there?
faqs.a: Sales of real property, including mineral interests, located in Michigan can trigger Michigan tax obligations regardless of where the seller lives. Talk to your own CPA or tax advisor about how the sale affects your specific tax situation before closing.

items.name: Trust-Owned Minerals
items.meta: Managing a Michigan mineral interest held in a family trust? Here's what trustees need to confirm before selling, from trust authority to beneficiary duties.

sections.html:
The trust document names you trustee, the trust holds a Michigan mineral interest, and now you're the one deciding what to do with an asset you didn't choose to own.

Family trusts pick up mineral interests the same way estates do, usually because the original owner set up the trust to manage land and other assets for the benefit of children or grandchildren, and a small Antrim or Niagaran interest got folded in along with everything else. Now, as trustee, you're on the hook for managing it prudently, which for a lot of trustees means dealing with an asset class they've never handled before: royalty statements, division orders, decline curves, none of it resembling the stocks and real estate that make up the rest of the trust portfolio.

Trustees have a fiduciary duty to manage trust assets for the beneficiaries' benefit, and that duty applies to a mineral interest the same as anything else in the trust. Sometimes that means holding a well-performing interest for the income stream it provides. Sometimes it means recognizing that a small, declining, or non-producing interest is more trouble than it's worth to manage and selling makes more sense for the beneficiaries than holding an asset nobody's actively watching.

sections.title: Confirming Trustee Authority to Sell
sections.html: Before selling, check the trust document for language specifically addressing the trustee's power to sell or manage mineral, oil, and gas interests. Most well-drafted trusts give the trustee broad authority over trust property, but some older or more restrictive trust documents limit what can be sold without beneficiary consent or court approval. If the trust is silent or ambiguous on mineral interests specifically, that's worth clarifying with the trust's attorney before proceeding, since selling without clear authority can expose a trustee to a beneficiary dispute down the road.

sections.title: Fiduciary Duty and Getting a Defensible Valuation
sections.html: A trustee's decision to sell needs to hold up if a beneficiary ever questions it, which means getting a documented, production-based valuation matters more here than in a straightforward personal sale. We provide a written valuation grounded in recent royalty history, the well's decline trajectory, and current operator status, which gives you something concrete to show beneficiaries or a probate court if the trust's administration is ever reviewed. That documentation is part of what protects a trustee acting in good faith, separate from whatever number the sale ultimately lands on.

sections.title: Multiple Beneficiaries, One Decision
sections.html:
Unlike an outright inherited interest where each heir can decide individually, a trust-owned mineral interest is typically one asset with one decision point, the trustee's, even when there are multiple beneficiaries with different preferences. Some beneficiaries may want the trust to hold the interest for ongoing income; others may prefer the trust liquidate it and distribute or reinvest the proceeds. As trustee, your job is weighing what's prudent for the trust as a whole and the terms of the trust document, not necessarily what any single beneficiary personally prefers, though keeping beneficiaries informed of the decision and the reasoning behind it is generally good practice regardless of what the trust requires.

If the interest is small, declining, or non-producing, the administrative cost of managing it as a trust asset, tracking 1099s, division order updates, annual reporting, often outweighs what it contributes to the trust, which is a legitimate factor in deciding to sell separate from the raw valuation number.

faqs.q: Does the trust document need to specifically mention mineral rights to sell them?
faqs.a: Not always, most trusts with broad property management powers cover mineral interests implicitly, but some older or more restrictive trusts limit sales without beneficiary consent. Check the specific trust language with the trust's attorney before proceeding.

faqs.q: Do all beneficiaries need to approve a trustee's decision to sell?
faqs.a: Generally no, if the trustee has clear authority under the trust document, though keeping beneficiaries informed is good practice. If the trust requires consent for asset sales, that requirement needs to be followed regardless of the trustee's general authority.

faqs.q: Why does a trustee need a formal valuation instead of just accepting an offer?
faqs.a: A trustee's fiduciary duty means decisions need to be defensible if ever questioned by beneficiaries or a court. A documented, production-based valuation protects the trustee by showing the sale price was grounded in real data, not an arbitrary or convenient number.

faqs.q: What happens to sale proceeds from a trust-owned mineral interest?
faqs.a: Proceeds stay in the trust and are distributed or reinvested according to the trust's terms, the same as any other trust asset sale. That's governed by the trust document, not by the mineral sale itself.

faqs.q: Should a successor trustee re-check an older valuation before selling?
faqs.a: Yes. Production, decline rate, and operator status all change over time, so a valuation from several years ago shouldn't be relied on for a current sale decision. Get a fresh, production-based number before finalizing anything on behalf of the trust.

faqs.q: Can a co-trustee block a sale the other trustee wants to make?
faqs.a: If the trust names co-trustees, most trust documents require joint agreement on major asset decisions unless the document specifically grants one trustee independent authority. Check the trust's language on co-trustee decision-making before assuming either trustee can act alone on a mineral sale.

items.name: Selling for Liquidity
items.meta: Need cash from your Michigan mineral rights for medical bills, retirement, or debt? Get a fast, straight valuation without a slow drawn-out process.

sections.html:
The roof needs fixing, a medical bill just landed, or retirement isn't stretching as far as planned, and that Antrim interest sitting quiet in a drawer suddenly looks like real money you could actually use.

There's a version of mineral ownership that works fine when you don't need the money: the check comes, you deposit it, life goes on. But plenty of owners hit a point where a slow trickle of quarterly or annual royalty income isn't what the situation calls for. Medical bills don't wait for a well's next production cycle. Retirement accounts sometimes need topping up faster than a fractional interest can provide. Debt with real interest accruing on it doesn't care that your mineral rights are theoretically worth something someday. When cash is the actual need, converting a mineral interest into a lump sum is a straightforward, legitimate move, and there's no reason to feel bad about prioritizing your own situation over holding an asset indefinitely.

The key when you're selling out of genuine need for liquidity is not letting the urgency get exploited. Buyers can tell when someone's motivated to close fast, and a fair buyer prices the interest the same way regardless of your timeline. An unfair one leans on that urgency to lowball. Knowing what your interest is realistically worth before you're under pressure to accept anything is the single best protection against getting shorted when you actually need the cash.

sections.title: How Fast a Sale Can Actually Move
sections.html: Once ownership and the well's production are confirmed, a straightforward mineral rights sale in Michigan can close considerably faster than most other real estate transactions, because there's no financing contingency, no buyer mortgage approval, no inspection period the way a house sale has. If your title is clean and your fractional interest is clearly documented, the main variable is how fast you can get paperwork back to us. For owners under real time pressure, that speed matters more than squeezing out the last percentage point on the offer.

sections.title: Getting a Fair Number Even Under Pressure
sections.html: We price based on the same inputs regardless of your circumstances: recent production history, the well's decline trajectory, current operator status, and what comparable interests have traded for. Your timeline doesn't change that math, and it shouldn't. If you're getting quotes from multiple places while you're under pressure, that's smart, and a legitimate buyer won't discourage you from checking. What you want to watch for is anyone using phrases like limited-time or today-only to rush a decision. Real production-based value doesn't have an expiration clock on it.

sections.title: Partial Sales Are an Option Too
sections.html:
If you don't need to liquidate the whole interest, selling a portion, say a percentage of your royalty interest for a set number of years, or a fractional split of the acreage, can raise the cash you need while keeping some ongoing income. This isn't right for every situation, since it adds complexity to the paperwork and division orders going forward, but for an owner who needs, say, enough to cover a specific bill without giving up the entire long-term asset, it's worth asking about rather than assuming an all-or-nothing sale is the only option.

Whatever you decide, get the number in writing before you commit to anything, and don't let a tight personal timeline talk you into skipping the basic step of confirming what the interest is actually worth first.

faqs.q: How fast Can you actually get cash from selling your mineral rights?
faqs.a: Faster than most real estate transactions since there's no financing or mortgage contingency involved. Once title and production are confirmed, the main factor is how quickly paperwork moves on your end, which owners under time pressure can often turn around quickly.

faqs.q: Will you get a worse price if you need to sell fast?
faqs.a: You shouldn't, if the buyer is pricing off actual production data rather than your timeline. A fair valuation is the same whether you're in a hurry or not. Be cautious of anyone using urgency tactics like limited-time offers, since real value doesn't expire on a countdown.

faqs.q: Can you sell just part of your mineral interest instead of all of it?
faqs.a: Often yes, either a percentage of the interest or a term-limited royalty share, which raises cash while keeping some ongoing income. It adds complexity to future paperwork, so it's worth discussing whether a partial or full sale better fits your specific need.

faqs.q: Is selling for liquidity a bad financial decision?
faqs.a: Not inherently. If you need cash now more than you need a small, uncertain trickle of future royalty income, converting the interest to a lump sum is a reasonable financial choice, not something to second-guess just because the asset could theoretically keep paying for years.

faqs.q: Will selling your mineral rights affect your taxes or benefits?
faqs.a: A mineral sale can have tax consequences and, depending on your situation, could affect eligibility for certain need-based programs. Talk to your CPA or tax advisor before closing so you understand the full picture beyond the sale price alone.

items.name: Mineral Rights in Divorce
items.meta: Splitting Antrim or other Michigan mineral rights in a divorce settlement? Get a clear-eyed value read so you and your attorney aren't guessing on the number.

sections.html:
A mineral interest doesn't split cleanly down the middle like a checking account, and that's exactly why it turns into the sticking point in a lot of Michigan divorce settlements.

Divide the house, divide the retirement accounts, divide the cars, and then somebody's attorney asks what the mineral rights are worth and the room goes quiet. Michigan mineral interests, especially older Antrim Shale royalty positions, aren't traded on an exchange with a daily price. There's no app to check. If a couple owns a fractional interest that's been sitting in the family since a lease got signed in the eighties or nineties, that interest still has to get a number attached to it before a settlement can move forward, and neither spouse's guess is going to hold up.

We work with divorcing owners and their attorneys the same way we'd work with anyone deciding whether to sell: pull the recent royalty history, check who the current operator is, look at where the well sits on its production curve, and land on a number that reflects what the interest is actually producing now, not what somebody remembers it making years ago. Sometimes that number becomes the basis for one spouse buying the other out. Sometimes it becomes the basis for an outright sale and a clean split of cash. Either way, the settlement needs a real figure, not a shrug.

sections.title: Buyout vs. Sale, Two Different Roads
sections.html: One spouse can keep the mineral interest and pay the other their share based on a fair valuation, which keeps the asset in the family and avoids selling something with ongoing production. That works fine when one party actually wants to keep managing division orders and tax paperwork on a fractional Antrim interest for the next twenty years. A lot of people don't want that job, especially post-divorce when they're already untangling shared finances. In that case, selling the whole interest and splitting the proceeds per the settlement terms is usually the cleaner path, and it closes the book on one more shared asset instead of leaving an ongoing financial tie between two people who are trying to separate their lives.

sections.title: Getting a Number Both Sides Can Trust
sections.html: The fastest way to blow up a settlement negotiation is for one spouse's attorney to pull a number out of the air and the other side's attorney to reject it on sight. We provide a written valuation based on actual production data pulled from the well's operator filings and recent statements, which gives both attorneys something concrete to work from instead of dueling guesses. It's not a courtroom appraisal, but it's grounded in real numbers, and that's usually enough to move a negotiation forward without dragging in a formal expert witness and burning legal fees neither side wants to spend on a fractional mineral interest.

sections.title: Timing Matters More Than People Expect
sections.html:
Divorce settlements have deadlines the mineral market doesn't care about. If the court is expecting a property settlement agreement by a certain date, waiting around for gas prices to move or hoping a well gets recompleted isn't a strategy, it's a delay. We can turn a written offer around fast enough to fit inside a normal settlement timeline, which matters when your attorney is trying to close out the case instead of leaving one asset dangling for months while everything else in the divorce is finalized.

There's also a practical wrinkle specific to Michigan Antrim interests: if the well is well into its decline, waiting doesn't typically make the number bigger. Unlike a house that might appreciate while a divorce drags on, a mature declining well is usually worth less the longer everyone waits, not more. That's a real factor for whichever spouse is trying to buy the other out, and worth putting in front of your attorney early rather than late.

faqs.q: Can mineral rights be split 50/50 between divorcing spouses?
faqs.a: Technically yes, but splitting an already-fractional Antrim interest into two even smaller slivers usually just creates two owners tracking tiny royalty checks. Most couples find it cleaner for one spouse to buy out the other's share at a fair valuation, or to sell the whole interest and split the cash per the settlement.

faqs.q: Who determines the value of mineral rights in a Michigan divorce?
faqs.a: There's no set formula the court applies automatically. Typically one or both attorneys request a valuation based on the well's recent production history and current operator status, and that number becomes the basis for negotiation, similar to how a home appraisal works for real property.

faqs.q: Does the mineral interest count as marital property if it was inherited?
faqs.a: That depends on Michigan property law and the specifics of your situation, including whether the interest was commingled with marital assets. That's a legal question for your divorce attorney, not something we weigh in on, but once the legal status is settled we can help put a real production-based number on the interest.

faqs.q: What if the well's production has been declining for years?
faqs.a: That gets factored into the valuation directly. A mature, declining Antrim well is worth a real number, just a smaller one than it was in its early producing years, and any honest valuation reflects that trend rather than pricing off an old high-production year.

items.name: Mineral Rights
items.meta: Own mineral rights under Michigan land? Learn what that ownership actually includes, how it differs from surface land, and what it's worth to sell.

sections.html:
Owning the minerals under a piece of Michigan land is a different thing entirely from owning the land itself, and a lot of owners find that out the hard way when they try to explain it to somebody.

Mineral rights are ownership of whatever's below the surface, oil, gas, and in some cases other minerals, separate and distinct from ownership of the surface itself. In Michigan, especially across the Antrim Shale and Niagaran reef trend counties, it's common for the minerals to have been severed from the surface decades ago, sometimes by the original homesteader who sold the farm but kept the minerals, sometimes the reverse, sold the minerals and kept the land. That severance means today's surface owner and today's mineral owner are often two completely different people, sometimes never having met, connected only by a legal description at the county register of deeds.

If you own mineral rights, what you actually have is the right to explore for and produce oil and gas from that tract, or, more commonly, the right to lease those minerals to an operator who does the drilling and pays you a royalty on production. You don't own a piece of dirt you can walk on and call yours. You own a legal interest in whatever's underneath it, and that interest is bought, sold, leased, and inherited independently of the surface.

sections.title: What Full Mineral Ownership Actually Includes
sections.html: Owning mineral rights outright, sometimes called owning the fee mineral estate, gives you the right to lease those minerals to an operator, negotiate lease terms including bonus payment and royalty rate, and receive royalty income once a well on your tract or unit produces. It also generally gives you the right to grant or withhold surface access for drilling if you happen to also own the surface, though in split-estate situations the surface owner typically has separate rights the mineral owner has to work around under Michigan law. Most Michigan mineral owners today aren't actively negotiating leases themselves; they inherited an interest already under lease, with an operator already producing, and their role is mostly collecting royalty checks and staying current with the operator.

sections.title: How Michigan Mineral Ownership Usually Got Fragmented
sections.html: The Antrim boom of the eighties and nineties leased and drilled across enormous swaths of northern Michigan, and every one of those original mineral owners has since had decades to pass the interest down through wills, intestate succession, and probate. What started as one person's ownership of, say, 80 net mineral acres under a farm has often become a dozen or more heirs each holding a small fraction of that original interest. If you're trying to figure out exactly what you own, the county register of deeds in the county where the minerals sit is the authoritative source, not old family paperwork or what a relative told you at some point.

sections.title: Selling a Mineral Interest
sections.html:
Selling mineral rights means transferring your ownership interest permanently via a mineral deed, in exchange for a one-time payment instead of ongoing royalty checks. Value depends on whether the interest is currently producing, leased but undrilled, or non-producing, along with the specific well's decline trajectory if it's producing, and comparable recent activity if it's not. There's no flat statewide number per acre that applies across Michigan; a producing Antrim interest, an undrilled Niagaran-trend tract, and a dormant fringe-county interest are three very different valuations, and anyone quoting a single number without asking about your specific situation isn't doing real analysis.

You can also sell only part of your mineral interest, a percentage, or a term-limited royalty share, if you'd rather keep some ongoing exposure while raising cash on part of it. That flexibility is worth knowing about before assuming a sale has to be all-or-nothing.

faqs.q: What's the difference between owning mineral rights and owning the land?
faqs.a: Mineral rights are ownership of what's below the surface, oil and gas primarily. Surface rights are ownership of the land itself. In Michigan these are commonly severed and owned by two different people, especially on land that's been in a family for generations since the Antrim boom leased widely across the state.

faqs.q: How do you find out exactly what mineral rights you own in Michigan?
faqs.a: Start with the county register of deeds in the county where the minerals are located. That record shows the legal description and recorded ownership, which is more reliable than old family documents, especially after multiple generations of heirship.

faqs.q: Can you sell mineral rights without owning the surface land?
faqs.a: Yes. Mineral rights and surface rights are separate legal estates in Michigan, and mineral rights can be sold, leased, or inherited independently of whoever owns the surface above them.

faqs.q: Is there a standard price per acre for Michigan mineral rights?
faqs.a: No, and be wary of anyone quoting one without reviewing your specific interest. Value depends heavily on whether the interest is currently producing, leased but undrilled, or dormant, and on the specific well's production trend if applicable.

items.name: Royalty Interests
items.meta: Own a royalty interest tied to Michigan production? Learn what a royalty interest actually is, how checks get calculated, and what it's worth to sell.

sections.html:
Every quarter or month a check shows up with a bunch of numbers you don't fully understand, and somewhere in there is your actual royalty interest, if you can find it.

A royalty interest is your share of oil and gas production revenue, free of the costs of drilling and operating the well, in exchange for having leased your mineral rights to an operator. When a Michigan mineral owner signs a lease, they typically retain a royalty, commonly a fraction like 1/8th historically or higher on more modern leases, meaning the operator keeps the rest of production revenue to cover drilling costs, operating expenses, and profit, while the royalty owner gets their cut without having paid a dime toward getting the well drilled or keeping it running.

Most Michigan mineral owners today hold a royalty interest rather than actively negotiating leases, because the lease was already signed, sometimes decades ago by a parent or grandparent, and what got passed down is the ongoing right to royalty checks on whatever the well produces. Understanding what that royalty fraction is, how it's calculated against gross production, and whether deductions are being taken for post-production costs is the starting point for figuring out whether your checks look right, and for valuing the interest if you're thinking about selling.

sections.title: How Royalty Checks Actually Get Calculated
sections.html: Your royalty check is your fractional share, say 1/8th or 3/16ths depending on your specific lease, multiplied by the gross value of production from the well or unit, sometimes reduced by post-production costs like gathering, compression, and transportation depending on how your specific lease was written. Two owners with the identical royalty fraction can see different net checks if one lease allows post-production deductions and the other doesn't. If your check seems low relative to what you understand the well's gross production to be, that deduction language in your original lease is usually the first place to look, not necessarily an error by the operator.

sections.title: Why Royalty Fractions Vary So Much Across Michigan
sections.html: Leases signed during the height of the Antrim boom in the eighties and early nineties often carried lower royalty fractions than leases signed more recently, simply because lease terms across the industry have generally trended toward higher landowner royalties over time as competition for acreage increased. If your family's interest traces back to an original 1980s lease, don't assume your royalty fraction matches what a neighbor with a more recently signed lease receives, even on comparable production. The fraction is fixed at whatever the original lease specified and generally doesn't renegotiate itself upward just because market norms shifted since then.

sections.title: Selling a Royalty Interest
sections.html:
Selling a royalty interest means transferring your right to future production income for a lump sum today, and the valuation hinges on your specific royalty fraction, the well's current production and decline curve, and whether post-production deductions are being taken, since that affects your actual net income stream more than the headline fraction does. We pull your recent statements and the well's production history to build a defensible number, and we'll walk you through exactly how we got there rather than just handing you a figure and asking you to trust it.

If your royalty interest is tied to a mature Antrim well that's well into its decline, expect the valuation to reflect that trajectory honestly. A royalty interest on a well making a fraction of what it made fifteen years ago is worth a real number today, just not the number a naive calculation off historical peak production would suggest.

faqs.q: What royalty fraction do most Michigan mineral owners have?
faqs.a: It varies significantly by when the lease was originally signed. Older Antrim-era leases from the 1980s and early 1990s often carry lower fractions than more recently negotiated leases. Check your original lease or division order for your specific fraction rather than assuming it matches a neighbor's.

faqs.q: Why are post-production costs deducted from your royalty check?
faqs.a: It depends on how your specific lease was written. Some leases allow the operator to deduct gathering, compression, and transportation costs before calculating your royalty; others don't. That language in your original lease determines whether your net check reflects gross or post-deduction production value.

faqs.q: How do you know your royalty check is calculated correctly?
faqs.a: Compare your royalty fraction and any deduction language in your lease against the gross production and deduction figures shown on your statement. If something doesn't add up, the operator's division order department can typically walk through the calculation with you.

faqs.q: What determines the sale value of a royalty interest?
faqs.a: Your specific royalty fraction, the well's current production level and decline trend, and whether post-production costs are being deducted. All three factor into what the interest realistically pays going forward, which is what drives a fair valuation.

faqs.q: Can you sell just part of your royalty interest?
faqs.a: Often yes, either a percentage of your fraction or a term-limited royalty share, letting you raise cash now while keeping some ongoing exposure. Ask us about structuring a partial sale if you don't want to give up the entire interest at once.

items.name: Non-Participating Royalty (NPRI)
items.meta: Own a non-participating royalty interest in Michigan? Learn what NPRI means, how it differs from owning minerals outright, and what it's worth to sell.

sections.html:
You get a royalty check but you never got a say in the lease, and now you're trying to figure out what kind of interest actually does that.

A non-participating royalty interest, NPRI for short, is a share of production revenue carved out of the mineral estate that comes with no right to lease, no right to negotiate bonus or royalty terms, and no right to receive delay rental or bonus payments the way a full mineral owner does. Whoever owns the underlying mineral estate handles all of that. The NPRI owner just receives their carved-out royalty share once production starts, based on the percentage or fraction specified when the interest was created.

In Michigan, NPRIs typically show up when a mineral owner sold or reserved a royalty share separately from the mineral estate itself, sometimes decades ago as a way to raise cash while keeping some future upside, or when an interest was divided that way during an estate settlement. If your paperwork describes a fixed royalty percentage with no mention of leasing rights or bonus payments, you're likely holding an NPRI rather than a full mineral interest, and that distinction changes both what you can expect from the interest and how it gets valued if you sell.

sections.title: NPRI vs. Owning the Full Mineral Estate
sections.html: The practical difference matters most when a lease comes up for renewal or a new operator moves into the area. A full mineral owner gets to negotiate the bonus payment, the royalty rate, and the lease terms directly. An NPRI owner has none of that leverage; they're locked into whatever royalty percentage was specified when the NPRI was created, regardless of what better terms a mineral owner might negotiate on future leases. If your NPRI was carved out at, say, a 1/16th royalty decades ago and today's typical Michigan lease royalty runs higher, you don't get the upside of that difference. You're stuck with the original fraction specified in your instrument, which is worth understanding clearly before assuming your interest works the same as a mineral owner's.

sections.title: How NPRI Value Gets Calculated
sections.html: Valuing an NPRI comes down to the specific royalty fraction you hold, the well's current production and decline trajectory, and how many years of production the interest realistically has left, similar in structure to valuing a mineral interest but working strictly off the fixed royalty percentage rather than any leasing upside. Because NPRI owners can't benefit from future lease renegotiation, the valuation is generally more straightforward, tied tightly to current and projected production, without the speculative premium a full mineral owner in an undrilled area might command.

sections.title: Selling an NPRI in Michigan
sections.html:
NPRIs are sellable the same as any other real property interest, transferred by a deed that specifically conveys the royalty interest, and buyers price them based on production data pulled from your specific well's operator statements. Because there's no leasing upside to factor in, an accurate valuation depends heavily on getting the exact royalty fraction and legal description right, which we confirm against the county register of deeds record before quoting anything. If your NPRI is tied to a mature, declining Antrim well, expect the number to reflect that decline the same way it would for a full mineral interest, since the underlying production trend drives both.

One thing worth checking before selling: confirm your NPRI hasn't reverted or terminated under any specific durational language in the original instrument, since some older NPRIs were created for a term of years or tied to a specific lease rather than granted in perpetuity. That distinction affects whether there's anything left to sell.

faqs.q: What's the difference between an NPRI and a mineral interest?
faqs.a: A mineral interest includes the right to lease and negotiate terms; an NPRI is just a fixed royalty share carved out of production with no leasing rights or say in lease terms. NPRI owners collect a set royalty fraction regardless of what a mineral owner negotiates on future leases.

faqs.q: Can an NPRI expire or terminate?
faqs.a: Some can, if the original instrument creating the NPRI specified a term of years or tied it to a specific lease rather than granting it in perpetuity. Check the original deed or reservation language, or have it reviewed, before assuming your NPRI is permanent.

faqs.q: How is an NPRI valued if you want to sell it?
faqs.a: Based on your specific royalty fraction against the well's current production and remaining decline trajectory. Since there's no leasing upside involved, the valuation ties closely to production data rather than speculative lease potential.

faqs.q: Do you need the mineral owner's permission to sell your NPRI?
faqs.a: No. An NPRI is a distinct, separately owned interest and can be sold independently of what the underlying mineral owner does with their interest.

faqs.q: How Can you tell if your NPRI is tied to a specific term instead of perpetual?
faqs.a: Check the original instrument that created the interest for any language limiting it to a set number of years or to a specific lease. If it's silent on duration, most NPRIs are presumed perpetual, but it's worth confirming rather than assuming.

items.name: Surface vs. Mineral Estate
items.meta: Confused whether you own the surface, the minerals, or both on your Michigan property? Here's how split estates work and what it means for selling.

sections.html:
Owning the farm doesn't automatically mean you own what's under it, and a lot of Michigan property owners find that out only after they try to sell one or the other.

Land in Michigan, like most oil and gas producing states, can be legally split into two separate estates: the surface estate, ownership of the ground itself, and the mineral estate, ownership of oil, gas, and other minerals below it.
