These two estates can be owned by the same person, which is called unified ownership, or they can be owned by two entirely different people, called a split estate, and Michigan has plenty of both, especially in Antrim and Niagaran-trend counties where the boom years of drilling triggered a lot of mineral severances that never got reunited with the surface.

If your family sold farmland decades ago but the deed specifically reserved the minerals, you might own mineral rights under land you haven't set foot on in years, owned now by strangers who live there or farm it. Or the reverse: you might own the surface of a piece of Michigan property and have no idea an operator has an active lease on minerals underneath it that were severed off before you or your family even bought the land. Both situations are common, and both require actually checking the record rather than assuming ownership works the way it feels like it should.

sections.title: How Split Estates Happen in Michigan
sections.html: Most Michigan split estates trace back to one of two moments: an original landowner selling the surface while specifically reserving the minerals in the deed, common when someone wanted to keep future oil and gas upside while cashing out of the farming operation, or an owner selling the minerals separately while keeping the surface, common when a landowner needed cash during a downturn and the minerals were the more liquid asset to sell off. Either way, once that severance happens and gets recorded, the two estates travel through separate ownership chains from that point forward, get inherited separately, and can be sold completely independently of each other.

sections.title: What the Mineral Owner Can and Can't Do on Someone Else's Surface
sections.html: Under Michigan law, the mineral estate is generally considered the dominant estate, meaning the mineral owner or their lessee has an implied right of reasonable surface use to access and develop the minerals, even if they don't own the surface. In practice this means an operator can typically access a well site, build necessary roads, and conduct drilling operations on someone else's surface land under the lease's terms, subject to reasonable compensation for surface damages, which varies by lease and by whether a separate surface use agreement was negotiated. If you're a surface owner dealing with a mineral lessee's access, or a mineral owner whose surface owner is pushing back on access, that's a real legal dynamic worth understanding, and a lease's specific surface use language matters a lot in how it plays out.

sections.title: Selling One Estate Without the Other
sections.html:
Mineral rights and surface rights are sold through completely different transactions and completely different markets. Selling your mineral interest doesn't touch your surface ownership at all if you happen to hold both, and vice versa. This is exactly what we handle, buying mineral interests, sometimes from owners who also own the surface and are keeping the land while selling just the minerals underneath, and sometimes from owners who inherited a mineral interest under land they've never owned or visited and have no reason to hold onto beyond whatever the royalty checks are worth.

Before selling either estate, confirm at the county register of deeds exactly what you own, surface only, minerals only, or both, and what the recorded legal description actually covers. It's not unusual for family paperwork to be vague on this point after a generation or two, and getting it wrong before a sale creates real problems down the line.

faqs.q: How do you know if you own the surface, the minerals, or both?
faqs.a: Check the recorded deed at the county register of deeds in the county where the property sits. It will show whether minerals were reserved or conveyed separately from the surface, and family paperwork alone often isn't reliable enough after a generation or two of inheritance.

faqs.q: Can an operator drill on your land if you don't own the minerals?
faqs.a: Generally yes, under Michigan law the mineral estate is typically considered dominant, meaning the mineral owner or their lessee has an implied right of reasonable surface access to develop the minerals, usually subject to reasonable compensation for surface damages under the lease terms.

faqs.q: Do you need to sell your surface land and mineral rights together?
faqs.a: No, they're completely separate transactions. You can sell mineral rights while keeping the surface, or sell the surface while keeping minerals, without one sale affecting the other.

faqs.q: What if you inherited mineral rights under land you has never owned?
faqs.a: That's common in Michigan's split-estate counties. Confirm your ownership and legal description at the county register of deeds, then decide whether to keep collecting any royalty income or sell the interest, entirely independent of who currently owns the surface.

items.name: Overriding Royalty Interests (ORRI)
items.meta: Own an overriding royalty interest tied to a Michigan lease? Learn how ORRI differs from a mineral royalty and what happens to it when a lease ends.

sections.html:
An overriding royalty interest looks like a mineral royalty on your statement, but it's actually tied to something entirely different underneath it, and that difference matters if you're thinking about selling.

An overriding royalty interest, ORRI, is a royalty carved out of the working interest under a specific lease, not out of the mineral estate itself. That's the key distinction most owners miss. Where a mineral owner's royalty exists as long as the minerals exist and gets renegotiated every time a new lease is signed, an ORRI is tied to one specific lease and typically expires when that lease terminates, whether it lapses, gets released, or the well is plugged and abandoned. In Michigan, ORRIs commonly show up when a landman, geologist, or small operator who helped put a deal together retained a small royalty carve-out as part of their compensation, rather than taking a cash fee, or when an operator assigned a portion of the working interest's royalty to a third party as part of a farm-out or sale.

If you inherited or acquired an ORRI, it's worth understanding clearly that your interest lives and dies with the specific lease it's attached to. That's different from a mineral or NPRI interest, which typically survives lease terminations and can be re-leased indefinitely by whoever holds the underlying mineral estate.

sections.title: Why ORRIs Are Tied to the Lease, Not the Minerals
sections.html: Because an ORRI is carved from the working interest rather than the mineral estate, it only exists as long as the lease creating it stays in effect. If the well the ORRI is attached to stops producing and the lease terminates under its own terms, or the operator releases the lease, the ORRI typically terminates along with it, with no automatic renewal the way a mineral owner's royalty resets on the next lease. This is the single most important thing to understand about ORRI value: you're not valuing a permanent claim on the minerals, you're valuing a royalty stream tied to the remaining life of one specific well and lease.

sections.title: Valuing an ORRI in a Mature Michigan Play
sections.html: Because ORRI value is capped by the remaining productive life of the specific well, valuation leans heavily on that well's current decline trajectory and how much production is realistically left before the lease naturally winds down. On a mature Antrim well decades into its decline, that remaining life might be modest, which puts a ceiling on what an ORRI tied to it is worth relative to a mineral interest that could theoretically be re-leased and redeveloped after this well's life ends. This isn't a knock on ORRI value, it's just a structural fact that any honest valuation has to account for rather than pricing an ORRI as if it were permanent like a mineral interest.

sections.title: Selling an ORRI
sections.html:
ORRIs transfer by assignment rather than a mineral deed, and buyers need to see the original instrument creating the override to confirm exactly what lease it's tied to and what percentage it carries. We pull the well's current production and compare it against the remaining term or expected life of the underlying lease to arrive at a fair number, and we'll tell you plainly if an ORRI's remaining value is limited because the well it's attached to is well into decline. That's more honest than pricing it as though the interest has decades of upside left when the structural reality says otherwise.

If you're not sure whether your interest is an ORRI, an NPRI, or a straight mineral royalty, the original instrument creating it will say. Terms like override, working interest carve-out, or assignment of royalty are the language to look for, versus a mineral deed or royalty deed language for the other interest types.

faqs.q: Does an overriding royalty interest last forever like a mineral interest?
faqs.a: No. An ORRI is tied to a specific lease and typically terminates when that lease ends, whether through natural expiration, release, or plugging of the well. A mineral or NPRI interest, by contrast, generally survives lease terminations and can be re-leased.

faqs.q: How do you know if you own an ORRI versus a mineral royalty?
faqs.a: Check the original instrument that created your interest. Language referencing an override, a carve-out from the working interest, or an assignment tied to a specific lease indicates an ORRI, versus a mineral deed or royalty deed for other interest types.

faqs.q: Why is your ORRI worth less than a similar-sized mineral interest?
faqs.a: Because its value is capped by the remaining productive life of the specific well and lease it's tied to, rather than the potentially indefinite life of the underlying mineral estate. On a mature, declining well, that remaining life, and therefore the ORRI's value, is more limited.

faqs.q: Can you sell an ORRI even if it might expire soon?
faqs.a: Yes, it's still a sellable asset, priced against the well's remaining expected production life. A fair valuation accounts for that remaining life directly rather than pretending the interest is permanent.

items.name: Working Interests
items.meta: Own a working interest in a Michigan well and tired of covering operating costs? Learn how WI differs from royalty and what it's worth to sell.

sections.html:
A royalty check just shows up. A working interest bills you first, and that difference catches a lot of Michigan owners off guard.

A working interest is fundamentally different from a royalty interest, and the difference matters a lot if you're trying to figure out what you actually own. Royalty owners collect a share of production revenue and never pay a dime toward drilling or operating costs. Working interest owners, by contrast, own a share of the well itself, which means they're on the hook for a proportional share of drilling costs, operating expenses, plugging liability, and every other cost tied to that well, in exchange for a proportional share of production revenue after expenses. It's ownership with real financial exposure attached, not passive income.

Working interests in Michigan often trace back to owners who were part of the original drilling deal, sometimes a small independent operator, a landman, or an investor who bought into a well when it was drilled decades ago, and that interest got passed down through inheritance the same way a royalty or mineral interest does. If you inherited what you thought was a simple royalty check and it turns out to be a working interest, you may have discovered that along with occasional revenue checks, you're also occasionally billed for your share of costs, workovers, plugging expenses, and other operating items that a royalty owner never sees.

sections.title: The Real Difference: Costs Alongside Income
sections.html: A working interest owner shares in both the upside and the downside of a well's economics. When the well is producing well and costs are low, that can mean a bigger net check than an equivalent royalty interest would provide, since there's no operator taking their share off the top before you get paid. But when costs spike, a major workover, a compliance issue, eventual plugging and abandonment, the working interest owner gets billed their proportional share, sometimes at inconvenient times with little warning. On a mature Antrim well decades into decline, plugging liability down the road is a real, non-trivial cost that a working interest owner needs to account for, since Michigan requires wells to be properly plugged when they stop producing, and that cost falls on working interest owners, not royalty owners.

sections.title: Why Owners Often Want Out of Small Working Interests
sections.html: A small fractional working interest inherited from a relative can be more headache than it's worth. You're getting periodic joint interest billing statements for your share of operating costs, sometimes owing money in a given month rather than receiving it, and carrying long-term exposure to plugging liability on a well that's well into its decline. Unless you're actively involved in the operation and want that exposure, a lot of inherited working interest owners find they'd rather convert the interest into a clean lump sum and be done with ongoing cost exposure entirely, especially on aging Michigan wells where the plugging bill eventually comes due regardless of how small your fraction is.

sections.title: Selling a Working Interest
sections.html:
Selling a working interest is more involved than selling a royalty or mineral interest because the buyer is taking on both future revenue and future cost exposure, including eventual plugging liability. That means valuation accounts for the well's remaining production, projected operating costs, and the timeline until plugging becomes necessary, netted against expected revenue. It's a more complete financial picture than a simple royalty valuation, and we walk through all of it with you so you understand exactly what's being priced and why.

If you've inherited a working interest and aren't sure whether it's actually a working interest or a royalty interest, check your statements: if you've ever received a bill for your share of costs rather than only checks, or if your paperwork uses language like operating agreement or joint interest billing, that's a working interest, not a royalty.

faqs.q: How do you know if you own a working interest or a royalty interest?
faqs.a: If you've ever received a bill for your share of drilling or operating costs, rather than only revenue checks, or your paperwork references an operating agreement or joint interest billing, that's a working interest. Royalty owners never pay operating costs.

faqs.q: Am you responsible for plugging costs on a working interest?
faqs.a: Yes, working interest owners share proportionally in plugging and abandonment costs when a well stops producing, since Michigan requires wells to be properly plugged. That's a real future liability worth factoring into whether you want to keep the interest.

faqs.q: Can you sell a working interest even with pending liability attached?
faqs.a: Yes. A buyer factors expected future costs, including eventual plugging liability, into the valuation alongside expected remaining revenue, so it's still a sellable interest, just valued on a fuller financial picture than a royalty interest.

faqs.q: Why did you get billed instead of paid on your working interest?
faqs.a: Working interest owners share in operating costs as well as revenue, so in months where costs like workovers or compliance expenses exceed production revenue, owners can receive a bill rather than a check. That's normal for working interests and different from how royalty ownership works.

items.name: Antrim Shale Mineral Rights
items.meta: Own Antrim Shale mineral rights in northern Michigan? Get a straight read on what a well past its prime is actually worth today, no mailbox-offer games.

sections.html:
The Antrim boom happened before most of today's owners were even paying attention to their mail. Now the checks are smaller, and you're wondering what's left.

The Antrim Shale is the reason half of northern Michigan has a mineral rights owner in the family tree. Companies like Michigan Petroleum, Aurora Oil & Gas predecessors, and later Jordan Development and Savoy Energy drilled tens of thousands of wells across Antrim, Otsego, Montmorency, Grand Traverse, Kalkaska, and the counties around them starting in the early 1980s, and by the late 1990s it was one of the most drilled plays in the country by well count. Shallow, coalbed-adjacent gas, cheap to drill, and cheap to produce for a while. That well count is exactly why so many Michigan families are holding a small interest today.

The problem nobody warns you about going in is the decline curve. Antrim wells produce biogenic gas generated by bacteria working on organic shale near the surface, not the deep thermogenic gas you hear about in the Marcellus or the Permian. Biogenic wells start weak, ramp up for a couple years as water is pumped off to let gas flow, peak, and then decline hard. Most Antrim wells are decades old now and sitting well down the back side of that curve. If your royalty check from a well drilled in 1988 or 1994 looks like a fraction of what it was ten years ago, that's not a paperwork problem. That's the well doing exactly what an Antrim well does this late in its life.

sections.title: Why Antrim Checks Keep Shrinking
sections.html: A typical Antrim well can produce for twenty, thirty, even forty years, but the volume in year thirty is nowhere close to the volume in year five. Operators aren't required to explain that to you every quarter, and the statement just shows gross MCF and a check amount. If you've been holding the interest a long time, you've probably watched the number drift down and wondered if you're being shorted. Usually you're not. You're watching a mature Antrim decline do what it does. That's useful context whether you decide to keep the interest or sell it, because a buyer pricing your interest is going to run that same decline math, not the number your grandfather's checks used to show.

sections.title: Who's Still Operating in the Play
sections.html: The Antrim isn't dead, it's just consolidated. Names like Savoy Energy, Jordan Development, and a handful of smaller independents still operate legacy wells across the core counties, and some units still see workovers, recompletions, or the occasional infill well where spacing allows it. That matters for valuation two ways. If your unit has an active operator doing maintenance work, decline might flatten out some instead of falling off a cliff, which supports a better number. If the operator is a smaller outfit with a thin balance sheet, that's worth knowing too, because plugging liability and operator solvency both factor into how a buyer prices legacy Antrim paper.

sections.title: What Ownership Actually Looks Like Up There
sections.html:
Antrim country is heirship country. A lot of these interests trace back to land grandpa or great-grandpa held outright, minerals severed off decades ago when the play took off, then split among kids and grandkids through however many generations of intestate succession or simple wills. It's not unusual to find an interest that's a 1/32nd or 1/64th of a unit, spread across cousins who've never met, tied to a legal description nobody in the family has actually looked at since the original lease was signed. If that's your situation, the county register of deeds office in the county where the minerals sit, Otsego, Antrim, Kalkaska, Montmorency, wherever your tract lands, is where the real record lives. Pull it before you talk value with anybody.

Split estate is common up here too. Plenty of Antrim country was homesteaded, sold off, and resold with the surface going one direction and the minerals staying with the original family or getting sold separately down the road. If you inherited the interest and have no idea whether you own minerals under a specific parcel or a fractional share across a whole unit, that's normal, and it's exactly the kind of thing that needs a title check before anyone puts a real number in front of you.

sections.title: Selling a Declining Antrim Interest, Straight Talk
sections.html:
Here's the part a lot of buyers won't say plainly: a mature, declining Antrim interest is worth less per net mineral acre than it was fifteen years ago, and it's worth less than a newly producing well in an active shale play in Texas or Oklahoma. Anyone quoting you a number that ignores decline, or worse, quotes off your best historical check instead of trailing production, is either careless or working an angle. A fair number is built off recent royalty statements, the specific well's current decline trajectory, remaining reserve estimate, and what similar Antrim paper has actually traded for lately, not what the well made in a good year twenty years back.

That said, declining doesn't mean worthless. Some owners with small fractional interests and shrinking checks decide the mailbox money isn't worth tracking anymore, especially with multiple heirs splitting an already-thin check into slivers nobody can spend. If that's you, selling converts a fading, unpredictable trickle into one number you control now. Others hold on because a legacy well that's still paying something, even a small something, for another decade beats zero. Neither answer is wrong. Just don't let anyone rush you into a number without showing their math.

faqs.q: Why did your Antrim royalty check drop so much over the years?
faqs.a: Antrim wells produce biogenic gas that peaks early and then declines steadily for the rest of the well's life. A well drilled in the 1980s or 1990s is likely deep into that decline now, so a smaller check usually reflects normal production falloff rather than an error on the operator's part. Pull a few years of statements and look at the volume trend before assuming something's wrong.

faqs.q: Is Antrim Shale mineral rights worth selling if the well is old?
faqs.a: It depends on remaining reserves, current decline rate, and how many heirs are splitting the interest. A fractional share of a heavily declined well can still have value, just less per acre than an actively producing modern well. The honest way to find out is to have recent statements reviewed against the well's actual production history, not guess off an old good year.

faqs.q: Who operates most Antrim wells in Michigan today?
faqs.a: Savoy Energy and Jordan Development are among the independents still active on legacy Antrim units across counties like Otsego, Antrim, Kalkaska, and Montmorency, alongside smaller local operators. Your division order or most recent check stub will name the current operator of record for your specific well.

faqs.q: What if you only own a small fractional interest?
faqs.a: Common in Antrim country because interests have been divided across generations of heirs. A 1/32nd or smaller share is still a real, sellable interest, it just needs a title check at the county register of deeds to confirm the legal description and your exact fraction before anyone can price it accurately.

faqs.q: Should you sell now or wait for gas prices to move?
faqs.a: There's no promise either way, and depending on how far along the decline curve your well is, price recovery may not move your check as much as it would on a younger well. Weigh a fair current offer against a mature well's shrinking production trajectory rather than betting the check gets meaningfully bigger from here.

items.name: How to Sell Mineral Rights
items.meta: The actual steps to sell Michigan mineral rights, from confirming what you own to closing the deed, without the mailbox-offer runaround.

sections.html:
Selling minerals isn't hard once you know the order of operations. Most of the confusion comes from owners skipping steps because a postcard made it sound instant.

You've probably gotten a letter offering to buy your Michigan mineral rights, maybe more than one, and the numbers on those letters rarely mean much because they're sent before anyone checks what you actually own. Selling for real is a five-step process, and none of the steps are complicated on their own. Here's how it goes when it's done right.

sections.title: Step one: confirm what you actually own
sections.html:
Before any number matters, someone has to establish your net mineral acres and your royalty or working interest, tied to a legal description that matches the county record. If you inherited a fraction of a fraction from a farm your grandparents owned, that math isn't always obvious from memory. This is usually the first thing a serious buyer does, pulling your deed history and any probate record to land on a real ownership figure.

If your minerals sit under an existing well, your division order does most of this work for you, since the operator already calculated your decimal interest.

sections.title: Step two: figure out if it's producing or not
sections.html:
Michigan mineral value splits into two very different categories. Producing minerals under an active Antrim or other well have real royalty history to point to, and that history, along with the well's decline stage, drives the offer. Non-producing or undeveloped minerals are valued more on lease potential and nearby activity, which usually means a lower number and more uncertainty, because there's no check stub proving anything.

Ask any buyer straight out which bucket your tract falls into and how that's shaping their number. A straight answer here tells you a lot about who you're dealing with.

sections.title: Step three: get more than one offer
sections.html:
This is the step most owners skip, and it's the one that costs them the most. Mailbox offers are built to be the only number you see, timed to arrive when a well just started producing or right after a lease bonus check, when owners are most likely to jump. Getting a second or third opinion costs you nothing but a little time, and it either confirms the first offer was fair or shows you it wasn't.

Offers on producing minerals are typically quoted as a multiple of recent monthly royalty income, adjusted for the well's decline curve and how much life it likely has left. That multiple moves with commodity prices and well performance, so don't expect the same number twice from two different buyers, or from the same buyer six months apart.

sections.title: Step four: understand what you're signing
sections.html:
A mineral deed transfers ownership permanently, which is different from a lease. Read the legal description carefully and make sure it matches your actual tract, not a rounded-off version of it. Some buyers try to slip in surface rights or executive rights language that goes beyond the minerals themselves, so it's worth a careful read or a quick attorney check before you sign, especially on a first sale.

If you're only selling part of your interest, or selling to different buyers for different tracts, the deed needs to reflect exactly that fraction, not your whole ownership.

sections.title: Step five: close and record
sections.html:
Closing on a mineral sale is simpler than a house closing. There's typically no walkthrough, no inspection, and no financing contingency, since most buyers pay cash. The deed gets recorded with the county Register of Deeds, and if you're selling minerals under a producing well, you'll want to notify the operator so future royalty checks go to the buyer instead of you.

Keep a copy of the recorded deed for your own records, along with the closing statement showing the sale price. Both matter later when it's time to figure your cost basis for tax purposes, and they're the easiest documents to hand a CPA if questions ever come up down the road.

faqs.q: How long does selling mineral rights actually take?
faqs.a: Producing minerals with clean title can close in a couple of weeks. Undeveloped minerals or anything with a title gap, like an unresolved estate, can take longer while that gets sorted out.

faqs.q: Do you have to sell all of your mineral interest?
faqs.a: No. Owners commonly sell a portion and keep the rest, or sell one tract and keep another. Any offer should specify exactly what fraction is being purchased.

faqs.q: Is there a minimum acreage to sell?
faqs.a: Not really. Buyers regularly purchase small fractional interests inherited through several generations of heirs, even down to a fraction of an acre.

faqs.q: What happens to your royalty checks after you sell?
faqs.a: Once the deed is recorded and the operator is notified, future royalty payments go to the new owner starting with the next production month, or as specified in the deed's effective date.

faqs.q: Should you talk to a lawyer before selling?
faqs.a: It's not required for most straightforward sales, but if title is unclear, the estate wasn't probated, or you're unsure about the legal description, a short consult with an attorney is worth the cost.

faqs.q: What if your minerals are undeveloped with no well on them?
faqs.a: You can still sell, though the process leans more on nearby lease activity and drilling interest than production history, and the number will reflect that added uncertainty compared to a producing tract.

items.name: What Are Mineral Rights Worth?
items.meta: An honest breakdown of what drives Michigan mineral rights value, from Antrim decline stage to acreage, without a made-up per-acre number.

sections.html:
Anyone who quotes you a flat dollar figure before knowing your well's production history is guessing, or worse, hoping you won't ask how they got there.

There's no single answer to what Michigan mineral rights are worth, and anyone who tells you otherwise without asking a single question about your tract is skipping the part of the job that actually matters. Value moves with production history, decline stage, commodity prices, and whether the acreage is even developed at all. Here's what actually drives the number, in plain terms.

sections.title: Producing versus undeveloped, the biggest split
sections.html:
If your minerals sit under an active well, there's real royalty history to work from, and that changes everything. Buyers can look at your monthly production and build a real projection of what's likely left. If your minerals are undeveloped, with no well ever drilled on the tract, value depends almost entirely on nearby drilling activity and lease interest, which in a lot of Michigan counties has been slow for years. Undeveloped acreage typically commands less than producing acreage because there's nothing concrete to project, just potential.

This one distinction explains more of the gap between offers than anything else. If you're comparing two numbers from two different buyers, make sure you're comparing apples to apples on which bucket your tract falls into.

sections.title: Where the well sits on the Antrim decline curve
sections.html:
Antrim Shale wells decline steeply in their first few years, then settle into a long, low-volume tail that can stretch on for decades. A well early in that curve, still throwing off strong monthly volumes, is worth more per dollar of current royalty than a well twenty years in in the shallow tail, even if the tail well still produces something every month. This is exactly why value is typically quoted against recent royalty checks rather than as a flat number, it has to account for how much runway is realistically left.

Owners sometimes assume a well that's been producing for decades is a sign of strength. In reality, longevity on an Antrim well usually means it's deep into the tail, producing a fraction of its early output, which weighs on value even though the well is technically still alive.

sections.title: Commodity prices move the number too
sections.html: Gas prices swing, and Michigan Antrim production is overwhelmingly gas, so an offer made during a price dip can look meaningfully different from one made six months later when prices recover. This isn't a buyer being unfair, it's the price deck used in any projection shifting with the market. If you're not in a hurry, it's fair to ask a buyer how current prices are factoring into their number, and to understand that waiting doesn't guarantee a better price, it just trades one uncertainty for another.

sections.title: Acreage, ownership fraction, and lease terms
sections.html: Your net mineral acres and your royalty fraction, typically inherited from an original lease, set the ceiling on what any given tract can produce. A larger fraction with a stronger royalty rate is worth more than a small sliver of the same well, all else equal. If you're unsure of your exact net mineral acreage, that's usually the first thing worth confirming, since it's the multiplier on everything else in the calculation.

sections.title: County and position within the play
sections.html:
Not every county in the Antrim trend looks the same. Some sit closer to the core of the play with denser well spacing and stronger historical production, while others sit on the flank with fewer wells and thinner history to draw from. Otsego and Antrim counties, for example, have some of the longest production histories in the trend, which gives buyers more data to work with than a county with only a handful of older wells.

This positional difference is one more reason a flat statewide number never makes sense. Two tracts of identical size in different counties can carry very different value depending on the well density and production history around them.

faqs.q: Can you just tell you a price per acre?
faqs.a: Not honestly, no. Value depends on whether the acreage is producing, where the well sits on its decline curve, and current commodity prices, so any real number has to be built from your specific tract rather than a flat rate.

faqs.q: Is undeveloped acreage worth anything?
faqs.a: It can be, particularly in counties with active leasing or nearby drilling, but it's inherently more speculative than producing minerals and typically valued lower as a result.

faqs.q: Why do offers change over time on the same tract?
faqs.a: Commodity prices move, the well continues declining month to month, and buyer appetite shifts. An offer that was accurate six months ago may not reflect today's numbers.

faqs.q: Does a bigger royalty check always mean higher value?
faqs.a: Generally yes, but the decline stage matters just as much. A large check from a well early in its curve is worth more per dollar than the same check from a well deep into its tail with little runway left.

faqs.q: How do you know if your offer is realistic?
faqs.a: Get a second opinion. If multiple buyers land in a similar range after looking at your actual production history, that's a reasonable signal. A single unexplained number isn't enough to judge by.

items.name: Reading Your Royalty Statements
items.meta: A plain-English walkthrough of the Michigan royalty statement, from decimal interest to deductions, and what a declining number actually means.

sections.html:
A royalty statement is dense on purpose, packed with abbreviations nobody explains. Here's what each part actually tells you about your well.

Every month or quarter, operators send Antrim and other Michigan mineral owners a statement alongside the royalty check, and most owners glance at the total and toss the rest. That statement actually holds useful information, especially if you're trying to understand whether your well is holding steady or sliding down its decline curve. Here's how to read it.

sections.title: The header: well name, decimal interest, and production month
sections.html:
At the top you'll usually find the well name or number, your decimal interest, which is your fractional share of the well's total production, and the production month the statement covers, which often lags a month or two behind the check date. If you own interests in more than one well, each one typically gets its own line or its own section, so don't assume one number on the page covers everything you own.

Confirm the decimal interest here matches what's on your division order. If it's changed without explanation, that's worth a call to the operator.

sections.title: Volume and price columns
sections.html:
This section shows the gas or oil volume attributed to your interest for the month, along with the price per unit the operator received. Multiply the two and you get your gross value before deductions. Watching this line month over month, over a year or two, is the clearest way to see where your well sits on its decline curve, since Antrim wells settle into a long, gradual downward trend after their early years.

Price swings independently of the well itself, so a lower check some months reflects the market, not necessarily a failing well, while a steadily shrinking volume number reflects the well itself declining.

sections.title: Deductions: severance tax and post-production costs
sections.html:
Michigan levies a severance tax on oil and gas production, and that's typically deducted before your net payment is calculated, along with post-production costs like gathering, compression, or transportation depending on your lease terms. These deductions are standard and expected, but they're worth understanding since they explain why your net payment is meaningfully lower than the gross value line above it.

If deductions suddenly jump or a new line item appears that wasn't there before, it's fair to ask the operator's royalty department what changed.

sections.title: What a declining statement actually tells you
sections.html: A steadily shrinking check isn't a sign something's wrong, it's the normal life of an Antrim well playing out. These wells decline sharply in their first several years, then settle into a long, low-volume tail. If you're watching your statements trend down year over year and wondering what that means for the value of your interest if you sold, that decline stage is exactly what a buyer factors into any offer, and it's worth keeping a few months of statements on hand if you ever want that conversation.

sections.title: Keeping your own records straight
sections.html:
It's worth holding onto statements for at least a few years rather than tossing them once the check clears. A run of statements shows a trend, which is more useful than any single month, whether you're tracking how your well is declining, checking that your decimal interest hasn't changed unexpectedly, or preparing for a future sale where a buyer wants production history.

If your statements come electronically, save copies somewhere you'll actually find them again, and if you inherited a mineral interest, ask whoever managed it before you whether old statements exist anywhere. They're useful even years after the fact.

sections.title: When to question a statement
sections.html:
Most discrepancies are minor and get resolved with a phone call to the operator's royalty department. But if your decimal interest changes without explanation, a deduction category appears that wasn't there before, or your payment stops entirely with no notice, it's worth asking directly rather than assuming it will sort itself out.

Operators generally want accurate records as much as you do, since an ownership dispute costs them more time than a quick clarifying call. Don't hesitate to ask.

faqs.q: Why does your check amount change every month?
faqs.a: Both production volume and commodity price shift month to month, and your payment reflects both. Some months a price increase offsets a volume decline, and vice versa.

faqs.q: What if you stop receiving statements?
faqs.a: This can happen if the operator changed, if your interest was moved into suspense over a title question, or if the well was shut in. Contact the operator's royalty department directly to find out which applies.

faqs.q: Are the deductions on your statement normal?
faqs.a: Severance tax and reasonable post-production costs are standard across Michigan production. If deductions seem unusually high compared to prior months, it's reasonable to ask the operator for an explanation.

faqs.q: Can you use old royalty statements when getting an offer to sell?
faqs.a: Yes, and it's one of the most useful things you can hand a buyer, since real production history lets them build an honest projection instead of guessing.

items.name: Division Orders Explained
items.meta: What a Michigan division order actually says, why the decimal interest matters more than the acreage, and what to check before you sign one.

sections.html:
A division order shows up in the mail, asks for a signature, and most Michigan mineral owners sign it without reading past the top line. That's the mistake.

If you own minerals under a producing well in the Antrim trend or anywhere else in the Michigan Basin, sooner or later an operator sends you a division order. It's not the lease. It's not the deed. It's the document that tells the operator's accounting department how much of the well's revenue is yours and where to send the check. Get comfortable with what's on that page before you mail it back, because once it's signed, the operator treats it as your confirmation that the numbers are correct.

sections.title: What the decimal interest actually means
sections.html:
Every division order carries a decimal interest, something like 0.00184532. That number is your share of the well's production, calculated from your net mineral acres divided by the total spacing unit acreage, multiplied by your royalty fraction. It looks small because spacing units in Michigan can run 40, 80, or 160 acres, and you're one owner among however many heirs, co-tenants, or original allottees still hold a piece of that old farm parcel.

The decimal is the whole ballgame. If it's wrong by even a little, you're getting shorted every month for as long as that well produces. Compare it against your last deed or your prior division order if you have one, and if the acreage the operator lists for your tract doesn't match your title records, don't sign until someone explains the gap.

sections.title: Why Michigan title gets messy here
sections.html:
A lot of Antrim-era minerals trace back to farm severances from the 1930s through the 1980s, then passed through probate a generation or two without anyone updating the county record. By the time a division order shows up, the decimal interest the operator calculated has to account for every heir, every prior conveyance, and sometimes a life estate nobody remembers signing. Operators pull this from the Register of Deeds records in the county where the minerals sit, and old handwritten legal descriptions don't always match up cleanly with modern survey language.

That's the single biggest reason division orders get held up or come back with the wrong decimal. If your name is on the order but a sibling, cousin, or your late parent's estate hasn't been cleared through probate, expect the operator to hold your share in suspense until title is straightened out.

sections.title: Suspense, pooling, and the fine print
sections.html:
Read the bottom of the form. Most Michigan division orders include language about pooling or unitization, meaning your interest gets combined with neighboring tracts to form the spacing unit the well actually drains. That's standard and it's how Antrim wells have always been produced, but you want to see the unit description match what you were told when the well was permitted.

You'll also see a suspense clause, which lets the operator withhold payment if there's a title defect, a missing signature from another heir, or a dispute over the decimal. If your check has stopped or never started, suspense is usually why, and it's worth a call to the operator's division order department to find out exactly what document they're waiting on.

sections.title: If you're getting ready to sell
sections.html: Buyers ask for your most recent division order before they'll put a number in front of you, because it confirms the decimal interest is real and current. If you've got one, dig it out. If you don't, or if it's been years since the well was re-divisioned after other heirs sold out, that's not a dealbreaker, it just means whoever makes you an offer has to verify ownership through the county record first, which takes a little longer.

faqs.q: Do you have to sign a division order to get paid?
faqs.a: Most operators won't release payment until it's signed, though Michigan law generally doesn't let an operator refuse payment forever over an unsigned order once your ownership is otherwise confirmed. Still, sign a correct one promptly so your checks aren't held in suspense.

faqs.q: What if the decimal interest looks wrong?
faqs.a: Call the operator's division order analyst before you sign anything. Have your deed or prior order in hand and ask them to walk through how they calculated your share. Errors happen more often than you'd think, especially on older Antrim units with multiple heirs.

faqs.q: Does signing a division order affect your ability to sell?
faqs.a: No. A division order just confirms your payment share on existing production. You can still sell your mineral interest afterward, and a signed, current division order actually makes the sale go faster because it backs up your ownership claim.

faqs.q: Why did your division order change after your parent passed away?
faqs.a: Once probate closes and title moves to the heirs, the operator has to re-run the decimal interest to reflect the new ownership split. Each heir typically gets their own division order for their fractional share going forward.

faqs.q: Can an operator lower your decimal without telling you?
faqs.a: Not properly. Any change to your decimal interest should come with a new division order and an explanation, usually because additional acreage was added to the unit, additional owners were found in the title, or a prior calculation was corrected.

items.name: Documents You Need to Sell
items.meta: The real paperwork list for selling Michigan mineral rights, including deed history, probate records, and what to do if you can't find any of it.

sections.html:
Nobody keeps a folder labeled mineral rights. Here's what to actually go dig up before you talk numbers with a buyer.

Selling mineral rights in Michigan isn't complicated, but it does move slower without the right paper. Most owners inherited their interest and never saw the original deed, so this list is meant to tell you what matters, what's optional, and what a title company can chase down on your own without you tearing the house apart looking for it.

sections.title: The deed or the last recorded conveyance
sections.html:
This is the document that severed the minerals from the surface, or the most recent deed that moved your fractional interest to you. If you've got it, great, it speeds things up. If you don't, a title examiner can pull it from the Register of Deeds in the county where the minerals sit, since Michigan county deed records go back well over a century in most of the Antrim counties.

What matters most is the legal description on that deed matching the tract a buyer or an operator has on file. Old descriptions written by section, town, and range sometimes don't line up cleanly with how a parcel gets referenced today, and that's usually a title company fix, not something you need to solve yourself.

If your interest passed through several conveyances over the years, a buyer or title examiner will want to see the whole chain, not a single link. Each deed in that chain has to trace cleanly from one owner to the next, so a gap anywhere along the way, an unrecorded transfer or a missing signature, is worth flagging early rather than discovering it mid-closing.

sections.title: Probate and heirship paperwork
sections.html:
If you inherited the minerals, whoever's buying wants to see how title passed to you. That means a death certificate for the prior owner, letters of authority or the probate order if the estate went through court, or an affidavit of heirship if it didn't. Michigan allows small estates and affidavit procedures for modest interests, which is common with mineral fractions that never got formally probated because nobody thought they were worth the filing fee.

If several siblings or cousins inherited together, each person's share needs to trace back cleanly. That doesn't mean everyone has to sell at once, but a buyer will ask who else holds a piece of the same tract.

sections.title: Division orders and check stubs
sections.html:
If the minerals are under a producing well, your most recent division order and a handful of royalty check stubs are worth more than almost anything else on this list. They confirm your decimal interest, show which operator is paying, and give a buyer real production history to work from instead of guessing. If you never receive a check because the tract isn't currently producing, that's fine too, it just changes how the interest gets valued.

Don't have a division order handy? A tax ID number or an operator name from an old letter is usually enough for someone to look the well up in Michigan's public well records.

sections.title: Tax statements and current mailing information
sections.html: Most counties send a property tax statement for severed mineral interests, and that statement usually has the parcel number a title search needs. Keep it even if the amount owed is small. You'll also want your current mailing address and a copy of a photo ID ready for closing, since the deed transfer has to match your legal name exactly.

sections.title: Lease copies, if you have them
sections.html:
If your minerals are leased, a copy of the lease itself helps confirm the royalty rate and term you're working under, though it's not always required to sell. If you never received a copy or lost it years ago, the operator's landman file or the county Register of Deeds usually has a recorded version on file.

None of this paperwork needs to be perfect or complete before you start a conversation about selling. Bring what you have, and let a title examiner fill the gaps from the county record.

faqs.q: What if you can't find any paperwork at all?
faqs.a: That's more common than not. A title examiner can rebuild most of this from county records and probate files without you producing a single document, though it may take a little longer to confirm your exact ownership share.

faqs.q: Do you need a lawyer to gather these documents?
faqs.a: Not usually for the gathering itself. Where an attorney helps is if the estate was never probated and heirship needs to be formally established, or if there's a title dispute among family members.

faqs.q: Is a tax parcel number the same as knowing exactly what you own?
faqs.a: No, it points to the tract but not always to your exact fractional share. That's why deed history and probate records matter, they establish the decimal interest and not merely the location.

faqs.q: What if your name is misspelled on an old deed?
faqs.a: It happens constantly with mineral records that are decades old. A minor discrepancy is usually cleared with an affidavit at closing rather than a full correction deed, though your title company will tell you which route fits your situation.

items.name: How to Spot a Lowball Offer
items.meta: The tactics behind lowball mailbox offers on Michigan mineral rights, and the specific questions that expose a number that won't hold up.

sections.html:
A form letter with a deadline and a big round number is designed to get a signature before you ask a single question. Here's how to see through it.

If you own minerals in the Antrim trend, you've probably gotten one of these letters: a flat offer, no mention of your actual well, and a deadline pushing you to sign fast. Some of it's legitimate, some of it's a lowball built on the assumption you won't check. Here's what separates the two, and the specific things worth asking before you sign anything.

sections.title: The unsolicited flat number
sections.html:
If a letter names a dollar figure before ever asking about your decimal interest, your well's production history, or how long it's been on decline, that number wasn't built from your tract. It's a generic offer sent to a whole mailing list pulled from county tax records, designed to catch whoever signs first. Sometimes it's close to fair, sometimes it's well under what a careful appraisal would land on, but there's no way to know without asking how it was calculated.

A legitimate buyer can tell you exactly what data went into their number: recent royalty checks, the well's decline stage, current gas prices. If they can't or won't, that's your answer.

sections.title: Artificial urgency
sections.html:
Deadlines, expiring offers, and language like act now show up because urgency works against you, not for you. There's rarely a real reason a mineral offer has to be accepted within a week. Your ownership isn't going anywhere, the well isn't drying up in the next ten days, and a legitimate buyer's number shouldn't evaporate just because you took time to get a second opinion.

If anything, a buyer pushing hard for a fast signature before you can compare offers is often a sign they know the number wouldn't survive that comparison.

sections.title: Vague or missing math
sections.html:
Ask how the offer was calculated. A straight answer references your production history, a multiple applied to recent royalty income, or a decline curve projection. A dodge sounds like industry standard rate or we just know the market. Anyone offering to buy your minerals should be comfortable walking you through their reasoning, because the math behind mineral valuation isn't a trade secret, it's just underwritten by data most owners don't think to ask for.

This applies just as much to a high offer as a low one. An unexplained number, whatever direction it leans, is worth pressure-testing before you sign.

sections.title: What actually protects you
sections.html: Get more than one offer before you decide anything. Ask each buyer the same questions: how they calculated the number, whether they looked at your actual well's production, and what assumptions they used on price and decline. Compare the answers themselves, beyond just the totals. A fair offer holds up to that scrutiny. A lowball usually falls apart the moment you start asking specifics.

sections.title: Watch for legal description tricks
sections.html:
Some mailbox letters describe your tract with a fraction that's slightly off from what you actually own, sometimes rounded down, sometimes referencing an outdated acreage figure. It's easy to skim past this line and focus on the dollar amount, but the fraction listed is what the offer is actually based on. Compare it against your deed or your last division order before signing anything, and flag any mismatch before you sign, not after.

This isn't always deliberate, sometimes it's just outdated county data, but it's worth catching either way since it directly affects whether the number in front of you actually reflects what you own.

sections.title: When a low number is actually honest
sections.html:
Not every modest offer is a lowball. A well that's twenty years into its Antrim decline curve, producing a fraction of its early output, legitimately supports a smaller number than a well that just started producing. The difference between a lowball and an honest low offer isn't the size of the number, it's whether the buyer can explain how they got there using your actual production.

If a buyer walks you through the decline stage, the pricing assumptions, and the math, and the number still comes in modest, that's not a red flag by itself. Judge the process behind it, beyond the total alone.

faqs.q: Are all unsolicited mailbox offers scams?
faqs.a: No, some are legitimate, just generic and untailored to your specific tract. The problem isn't that they're unsolicited, it's that the number often wasn't built from your actual production or ownership details.

faqs.q: How many offers Should you get before deciding?
faqs.a: Two or three is usually enough to tell whether a number is in a reasonable range. If they cluster close together after each buyer reviews your actual production, that's a useful signal.

faqs.q: What if the offer letter says it's final and non-negotiable?
faqs.a: Treat that the same as a deadline, it's a pressure tactic. A real buyer's number is theirs to adjust if you bring new information, like a more recent royalty statement, to the table.

faqs.q: Is a higher offer automatically the honest one?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. A number that's unusually high with no explanation can be a bait tactic too, sometimes revised downward once you're further into the process. Ask for the math either way.

items.name: Mineral Deeds & Title Transfer
items.meta: How mineral deed transfers work in Michigan, from legal description problems to recording with the county, explained without the legal jargon.

sections.html:
A mineral deed looks like any other deed until you get to the legal description, and that's where most Michigan transfers actually get held up.

Transferring mineral rights in Michigan runs through the same county recording system as any other real property transfer, but the details that trip people up are specific to minerals: severed estates, fractional interests, and legal descriptions written before anybody imagined a computer would ever need to read them. Here's what actually happens when a mineral interest changes hands.

sections.title: What a mineral deed actually does
sections.html:
A mineral deed conveys ownership of the oil, gas, and mineral estate under a described tract, separate from the surface. In Michigan, mineral and surface ownership were commonly split, or severed, decades ago when a farmer sold the land but kept the minerals, or the other way around. Once severed, the mineral estate has its own chain of title that has to be tracked independently of who owns the surface today.

The deed itself is short, usually a page or two, but it has to correctly identify the grantor, the grantee, the legal description of the tract, and the fraction or percentage of the mineral interest being conveyed if it's not the full interest.

sections.title: Legal descriptions and why they cause problems
sections.html:
Michigan mineral tracts are typically described by section, township, and range, sometimes going back to descriptions written in the 1800s or early 1900s when the land was first platted. Over generations, as those tracts got divided among heirs or partially sold off, the descriptions in the county record can get inconsistent, missing an acreage figure, referencing a since-corrected survey, or splitting a fraction in a way that's hard to reconcile against a current deed.

A title examiner's job before any transfer is to trace that description back through every conveyance to confirm exactly what's being sold matches exactly what's on record. When this gets skipped, you end up with title gaps that surface later, sometimes when an operator tries to divisionize a new well and finds the ownership doesn't add up to one hundred percent.

sections.title: Recording with the county
sections.html:
Once signed and notarized, the deed gets recorded with the Register of Deeds in the county where the minerals sit. Recording is what makes the transfer effective against future claims and puts the new owner on the public record. Michigan counties in the Antrim trend, like Otsego, Antrim, Kalkaska, and Montmorency, each maintain their own recording office, and a deed has to be recorded in the correct county for the tract it covers.

If your interest spans multiple counties, which happens with larger inherited tracts, you may need separate deeds recorded in each county rather than one document covering everything.

sections.title: After the deed is recorded
sections.html: If the minerals are under a producing well, the new owner needs to notify the operator with a copy of the recorded deed so future royalty payments and division orders get redirected. This doesn't happen automatically just because the deed is on file at the county, operators typically require their own notification and paperwork before updating their payment records.

sections.title: Special situations that slow things down
sections.html:
A few scenarios come up often enough with Michigan mineral transfers that they're worth knowing ahead of time. If the interest is owned by an estate that never closed probate, the deed can't move until that's resolved or an affidavit of heirship covers the gap. If multiple heirs own a tract as tenants in common, each one's fractional share generally needs its own signature, even if only one heir is selling their portion.

Life estates, old mortgages that were never released, and unreleased prior leases can also show up on decades-old Michigan mineral tracts. None of these are usually deal-killers, they just add a step, and a title examiner's job is to spot them before closing rather than after.

sections.title: What a buyer typically covers
sections.html: In most direct-sale transactions, the buyer prepares the deed, handles the title search, and covers the recording fee with the county. Your job as the seller is mainly to review the document for accuracy, sign, and get it notarized. It's still worth reading it carefully rather than assuming the paperwork is boilerplate you can skip past.

faqs.q: How long does a mineral deed take to record?
faqs.a: Most Michigan counties process recordings within a few business days to a couple of weeks, depending on the office and how they're currently handling volume, whether that's in person, by mail, or electronically.

faqs.q: Do you need a title company for a mineral deed transfer?
faqs.a: It's not legally required, but a title company or attorney catches legal description problems and confirms clean title before recording, which prevents disputes down the road, especially with older or inherited interests.

faqs.q: What if the legal description on the old deed doesn't match today's records?
faqs.a: This is common with older Michigan mineral tracts and is usually resolved with a corrective deed or a title opinion that reconciles the descriptions rather than starting over.

faqs.q: Can you transfer just part of your mineral interest?
faqs.a: Yes, a deed can convey a specific fraction or percentage rather than your full interest, and this is common when owners sell part of an inherited tract while keeping the rest.

items.name: Lease vs. Sell: Which Is Right?
items.meta: Should you lease or sell your Michigan mineral rights? An honest look at Antrim decline curves, bonus payments, and what each path actually pays out.

sections.html:
Every mineral owner in the Antrim trend eventually asks the same question. Lease it and wait, or sell it and be done. There's no universal right answer, just tradeoffs.

Leasing and selling solve different problems. A lease keeps you in the game for whatever the well produces over its life, paid out a little at a time, with the risk and the upside both spread over years. A sale gets you a lump sum now, based on what a buyer thinks that future income stream is worth today, discounted for the fact that gas wells decline and nobody can promise what year fifteen looks like. Here's how to think through which one fits your situation.

sections.title: What leasing actually gets you
sections.html:
If your minerals are undeveloped, a lease usually comes with an upfront bonus payment per acre plus a royalty percentage on anything produced later, if anything ever is. That's the trade: cash now is small, but you keep the long-term upside if a well gets drilled and performs well. The catch is that a lot of Michigan mineral owners have been leased for decades without a single well ever going in on their specific tract, which means the bonus was the only money that ever showed up.

If you're already receiving royalties under an existing Antrim lease, there's often nothing to renegotiate unless the lease term is expiring or an operator wants to extend it, in which case you may have a little leverage on bonus or royalty terms for a new lease.

sections.title: What selling actually gets you
sections.html:
Selling converts your mineral interest, whether it's currently producing royalty income or sitting undeveloped, into one payment now. On producing tracts, that number is typically quoted as a multiple of recent monthly royalty income, adjusted for the well's decline stage, because a well six years into an Antrim decline curve is worth less per dollar of current royalty than a well that just came online. On undeveloped tracts, the number leans more on lease activity and drilling interest nearby, which in a lot of Michigan counties has been quiet for years, so don't expect an undeveloped fraction to command what a producing one does.

The tradeoff is real: once it's sold, you're out of any future upside, including a price spike, a workover that boosts production, or new drilling nearby. You're also out of any future downside, which matters more than owners think once a well is fifteen or twenty years into its life.

sections.title: The Antrim decline curve changes the math
sections.html:
Antrim Shale wells are known for a particular production pattern: a steep initial decline followed by a long, low-volume tail that can run for decades. That tail is real income, but it's also small and shrinking, and it makes the case for selling stronger the further along a well is in its life, because you're trading a long stretch of modest monthly checks for one number today rather than betting on the tail holding up.

On the flip side, if a well is early in its life or a new well was recently permitted nearby, the case for holding and collecting royalty income for a while longer gets stronger, since you're closer to the productive part of the curve.

There's no set year where selling suddenly makes more sense than holding, it's a gradual shift, and it's worth looking at your own trailing royalty statements to see roughly where your well sits before deciding either way.

sections.title: Questions worth asking yourself
sections.html: Do you need the cash now for something specific, or are you comfortable waiting on smaller monthly checks that could run for years or could taper off faster than expected? Is the interest spread across multiple heirs who'd rather split one payment than manage decades of small royalty checks between them? Is the tract producing at all, or has it been sitting undeveloped with no lease activity for years? None of these have a universal answer, but they're the ones that actually decide which direction makes sense for your situation.

faqs.q: Can you lease part of your minerals and sell the rest?
faqs.a: Yes. Owners with multiple tracts, or a fractional interest split among family, sometimes lease one piece and sell another depending on how each tract is producing.

faqs.q: If you is already leased, Can you still sell?
faqs.a: Yes. Selling a leased mineral interest is common, the buyer simply steps into your position under the existing lease and receives future royalty payments in your place.

faqs.q: Does selling mean giving up the mineral rights forever?
faqs.a: Yes, a mineral deed is a permanent transfer of ownership, unlike a lease which typically has a term and reverts back if drilling doesn't happen.

faqs.q: Which pays more, leasing or selling?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on how the well performs after the decision is made, which nobody can know in advance. Selling locks in a known number today, leasing bets on an unknown future.

faqs.q: Does an existing lease affect what a sale is worth?
faqs.a: Yes, an active lease with royalty history gives a buyer real production data to work from, which generally supports a more grounded valuation than an undeveloped tract with no lease at all.

items.name: Taxes When You Sell Mineral Rights
items.meta: How selling Michigan mineral rights is generally taxed, including capital gains and inherited basis, plus what to bring to your CPA.

sections.html:
Selling minerals triggers a tax question most owners haven't thought about since the interest showed up on a deed with their name on it.

This isn't tax advice, it's a plain-language overview so you walk into your CPA's office knowing what questions to ask. Selling mineral rights generally has different tax treatment than the royalty income you may have been receiving all along, and getting the basics straight ahead of time makes that conversation faster and cheaper.

sections.title: Capital gains, not ordinary income
sections.html:
When you sell mineral rights outright, the proceeds are generally treated as a capital gain rather than ordinary income, which is different from how royalty checks are typically taxed while you're receiving them. The gain is calculated as your sale price minus your cost basis in the minerals, and whether that gain is short-term or long-term depends on how long you're considered to have held the interest.

This distinction matters because capital gains rates are often more favorable than ordinary income rates, but the specifics depend on your full tax picture, which is exactly the kind of thing to run past a CPA before you sign anything.

sections.title: Inherited minerals and stepped-up basis
sections.html:
Most Michigan mineral owners didn't buy their interest, they inherited it, often from a parent or grandparent who held the same fractional interest for decades. Inherited property generally receives a stepped-up basis, meaning your cost basis is typically based on the fair market value at the time you inherited it, not what your relative originally paid or what the interest was worth generations ago.

That stepped-up basis can significantly reduce your taxable gain compared to what you might assume, since the clock effectively resets at inheritance. Establishing that value accurately for the date you inherited is worth doing carefully, and your CPA can advise on how to document it.

sections.title: Depletion and prior royalty income
sections.html:
If you were receiving royalty checks before selling, you may have already been claiming a depletion deduction against that income, which reduces your basis over time. That prior depletion factors into the basis calculation when you eventually sell, so your CPA will want your royalty history alongside your sale documents to get the calculation right.

This is one more reason it's worth keeping old royalty statements even after you've sold, in case questions come up later.

sections.title: What to bring to your CPA
sections.html: Gather your closing documents from the sale, any information on how and when you acquired the interest, whether by inheritance, gift, or purchase, and your royalty history if the minerals were producing before the sale. Handing your CPA a complete picture up front, rather than piecing it together after the fact, generally saves time and gets you a more accurate answer on what you owe.

sections.title: Multiple heirs and shared interests
sections.html:
When several siblings or cousins inherit a mineral interest together and each sell their own fractional share, each person generally handles their own tax reporting individually based on their own basis and their own proceeds. One heir's tax situation doesn't automatically apply to another, even though the underlying tract and the sale may have happened at the same time.

This is worth mentioning to your CPA specifically if your sale involved family members selling alongside you, since it affects how the paperwork gets organized and reported.

sections.title: State considerations
sections.html:
In addition to federal treatment, Michigan has its own state income tax considerations for gains from selling mineral rights. The specifics depend on your overall state filing situation, and your CPA is the right person to walk through how a mineral sale fits into your Michigan return alongside everything else.

None of this is meant to replace that conversation, just to help you walk into it with the right documents and the right questions ready.

sections.title: Timing a sale around tax planning
sections.html: Some owners think about whether closing a sale in December versus January changes their tax picture, and it can, depending on what else is happening in that tax year. This is exactly the kind of timing question worth raising with your CPA before you finalize a closing date rather than after, especially if you have other significant income or gains in the same year.

faqs.q: Do you owe tax the same year you sell?
faqs.a: Generally yes, the sale is typically reportable in the tax year the transaction closes, but talk to your CPA about your specific filing situation and any estimated payment requirements.

faqs.q: What if you don't know what the minerals were worth when you inherited them?
faqs.a: This comes up often. A CPA or appraiser can help establish a reasonable value as of the inheritance date using historical production and pricing data, which becomes your stepped-up basis.

faqs.q: Is selling mineral rights taxed differently than a lease bonus payment?
faqs.a: Yes, lease bonus payments are generally treated as ordinary income while an outright sale of the mineral interest is generally treated as a capital gain, so the two aren't interchangeable for tax purposes.

faqs.q: Should you talk to a CPA before or after you get an offer?
faqs.a: Either works, but talking to your CPA or tax advisor before you close gives you time to gather the right documentation and understand the tax picture without pressure to decide quickly.

items.name: How Minerals Are Appraised
items.meta: The methods buyers actually use to value Michigan mineral rights, from decline curve analysis to comparable sales, and why two appraisals rarely match.

sections.html:
Ask three buyers to appraise the same tract and you'll get three different numbers. That's not a scam, it's how mineral valuation actually works.

There's no MLS for mineral rights and no single accepted appraisal standard the way there is for a house. Instead, buyers lean on a handful of methods, weight them differently, and land on a number that reflects their own read of the well's future. Understanding those methods won't get you an exact price, but it will help you tell a serious offer from a lazy one.

sections.title: Decline curve analysis
sections.html:
For producing minerals, this is the method that carries the most weight. A buyer looks at monthly production history from the well, usually pulled from Michigan's public production records, and models how much gas or oil is likely left based on the decline pattern so far. Antrim wells in particular follow a well-documented curve: steep early decline, then a long, shallow tail that can run for years at low volume.

The value comes from projecting that remaining production forward, applying a price deck for gas or oil, and discounting future income back to today's dollars because a check you'll receive in year twelve is worth less today than a check you'll receive next month. Two buyers can run the same production history through slightly different price assumptions or discount rates and land on noticeably different numbers, and that's normal, not a red flag by itself.

sections.title: Recent royalty income as a shortcut
sections.html:
A faster, rougher method quotes an offer as a multiple of your trailing royalty income, usually averaged over recent months. It's less precise than a full decline curve model but it's quick, and it's the method most mailbox offers use because it doesn't require pulling well data at all. The multiple applied depends heavily on where the well sits on its decline curve, current commodity prices, and how much risk the buyer is pricing in.

If someone gives you a number without ever asking how your well is producing or how long it's been online, they're likely working off this shortcut, possibly with outdated assumptions.

sections.title: Comparable sales, when they exist
sections.html: In areas with a lot of transaction activity, buyers sometimes reference recent sale prices for similar tracts nearby, similar to how a realtor comps a house. Michigan's mineral market doesn't have the transaction volume of a Permian Basin county, so true comparables are harder to come by, and they get weighted less than production-based methods for that reason.

sections.title: Undeveloped minerals: a different calculation entirely
sections.html: Without production history, there's no decline curve to model. Value on undeveloped tracts leans on lease activity nearby, whether operators are actively drilling in the county, and general geological potential for the formation under your acreage. This is inherently more speculative, and offers on undeveloped minerals should reflect that uncertainty rather than promise a specific number as if it were as solid as a producing tract's appraisal.

sections.title: How your own paperwork factors in
sections.html:
The quality of the appraisal a buyer can offer you is only as good as the information they're working from. A recent division order or a stack of royalty statements lets a buyer run a real decline curve analysis instead of leaning on the rougher shortcut method. If your minerals are undeveloped, knowing your net mineral acres and the county your tract sits in still helps, even without production history to anchor the number.

This is why a serious buyer asks questions before naming a figure, and why an unsolicited letter with a flat number attached almost never reflects real appraisal work. If you want a more accurate number, come prepared with whatever documentation you have, even if it's incomplete.

sections.title: Getting a second opinion
sections.html:
Since no single appraisal method produces a perfect answer, comparing offers from more than one buyer is the closest thing to a real check on value that most owners have access to. If two or three buyers, working independently from your actual production history, land in a similar range, that's a reasonable signal the number reflects your tract fairly.

If the numbers vary wildly, ask each buyer to walk through their assumptions rather than picking the highest one by default. A number built on outdated production data or an aggressive price deck isn't necessarily the most accurate one just because it's the biggest.

faqs.q: Can you get a formal appraisal on your own before selling?
faqs.a: You can hire a petroleum engineer or reservoir consultant to run a decline curve analysis independently, though for smaller fractional interests the cost sometimes outweighs the benefit. Getting multiple buyer offers accomplishes something similar at no cost to you.

faqs.q: Why did two buyers give you such different numbers?
faqs.a: Different price decks, different discount rates, different assumptions about how much longer the well produces. It doesn't automatically mean one buyer is being dishonest, though it's always worth asking each one to explain their number.

faqs.q: Does the appraisal change if gas prices move?
faqs.a: Yes. Value on producing minerals is tied to the price deck used in the projection, so an offer made during a price dip can look different from one made when prices are higher, even on the exact same well.

faqs.q: Is a higher offer always the more accurate one?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Some offers are priced high to get a signature quickly and may not reflect a careful look at the well's decline stage. It's worth asking how the number was calculated regardless of whether it's high or low.
